During the last two weeks we have heard one Quebec member after another chiding the government because they were not keeping their promise of a moderate war effort. As a matter of fact this group have repeatedly stated their stand on the war, through the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. He pointed out in Septem-tem of 1939 that we had no confidence in the government that was controlling the British war effort at that time, either in their international policies or their war policies. That government changed; there came to power in Great Britain a new government, with a powerful labour influence, headed by a man in whom we all had confidence. The C.C.F. stated at that time, and have stated repeatedly since, their stand on the war; and the Minister of Agriculture is not playing the game when he tries to tie up the present amendment with statements made in September, 1939, when conditions i)t-ere totally different.
In this amendment we urge the government, if they are determined to proceed with the plebiscite, to add a second question in which we would have them ask:

The Address-Mr. Douglas (Weybum)
* ^re -vou *n favour of the conscription of war industries, accumulated wealth and financial institutions, at the same time and on the same basis of sacrifice as the proposed extension of the conscription of man-power?
We make this proposal for three reasons. The first is that we are convinced that a large section of the Canadian people are not prepared to support the conscription of manpower for overseas service unless it is accompanied by the conscription of wealth and vital war industries. The second is that we are convinced that the conscription of man-power in itself will not enable us to win the war. President Roosevelt has said that this war is going to be won or lost in the factories. As has been said so often, this is a mechanized war, in which the production of tanks, planes and modern equipment is an integral part of our war effort. A million men in uniform armed with rifles and machine guns, without the mechanized equipment essential to modern war, would be almost useless. This has become a war not of masses of men but of the productive power of entire nations; and to talk in terms of the conscription of manpower while leaving industry in its present haphazard condition would be to fight the war of 1942' with the mentality of 1914.
The third reason for proposing this subamendment is that we believe the government's oft-repeated promise of equality of sacrifice ought to be made a reality rather than a mere euphonious platitude.
In June, 1940, the National Resources Mobilization Act was before this house. It proposed to give the government power to conscript material and human resources. At that time some of us in this corner said we did not doubt that the government would use its power to conscript human resources, but we had neither confidence nor assurance that the government would use its power to conscript wealth or industry. It will be remembered that the Prime Minister was somewhat indignant; he repudiated the idea that he, the Prime Minister of Canada, would place more value on material things than on human life. However, the record speaks for itself. The National Resources Mobilization Act has been on the statute books of Canada for a year and a half. What industries have been conscripted under that act? What wealth has been conscripted? What financial institutions have been taken over? So far the government's legislation has been used for one thing; that is, the securing of man-power for home defence. To two successive budgets this group has moved an amendment calling for interest-free compulsory loans to be levied on the basis of ability to pay. Twice the government has rejected this proposal. It is becoming increasingly apparent that when the government talks about conscription it has in mind the conscription of man-power only, with wealth and industry left in the hands of those who operate them for private and personal gain. . If the government wants the whole-hearted cooperation of the great mass of the people of Canada, then it will accept this subamendment. If it is still determined to take a plebiscite it will give the man on the street a chance to express his opinion on this very vital matter. If the government refuses it can have only one meaning; that is, that it is afraid the question would be greeted with an overwhelming vote in the affirmative. I challenge the government to put this vote to the test and see.
I should like to touch very briefly on one or two things I believe ought to be done, in order that we may make a more effective contribution to the winning of this war. The first is that the government, having conscripted wealth and industry, ought to submit a plan for the utilization of our man-power similar to the one which has been outlined in Great Britain, as described in the Economist of December 14, 1941. The government ought to know the maximum number of men that can be spared from industry and agriculture for the fighting services. They should know, in turn, how the men available for the fighting services should be divided between the respective arms. The public should be told frankly that we cannot raise unlimited numbers of men for the army. At present six divisions are contemplated. Allowing two men in reinforcements for every man in an army division, that means we ought to have 50,000 men for each division, which would mean in the neighbourhood of 300,000 men. If we add to this number 150,000 men for the air force, 25,000 men for the navy and say 200,000 men required for the defence of Canada, we are getting close to 750,000 men, which may be the most we can spare from agriculture and industry without seriously affecting our contribution in these two important fields of operation. I do not know. It may be possible to take men out of agriculture and industry and replace them with women, but certainly the government ought to know. Some comprehensive plan ought to be placed before parliament and before the Canadian people if anything like an intelligent and united effort is to be obtained.
Another thing which must be done, in addition, is to provide for those with small fixed incomes who have been adversely affected by the increased cost of living and who have no means by which they can increase their income
526	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Douglas (Weybum)
proportionately. I refer particularly to the old age pensioners and soldiers' dependents, whose cost of living has increased in, the neighbourhood of 25 per cent on the basis of the commodities people commonly buy, and whose standards of living have had to be reduced to that extent. It does not help our war effort to have the parents and relatives of our men overseas feeling the pinch of poverty. Case after case has come to my attention of parents whose old age pensions have been stopped because their soldier sons have assigned part of their pay to them. Soldiers' dependents are receiving the same allowance now as they received in 1939 when the cost of living was much low'er than it is to-day. Canada's war effort can be strengthened by taking steps to remedy this lamentable situation.
Third, Canada's war effort can be assisted materially if the government will institute a new deal for agriculture. I do not propose at this time to go into the conditions of western agriculture. I did that on November 14 last and there will be opportunities for doing so again during the present session, but I want to say that it is to the everlasting disgrace of this government, and to the Saskatchewan members who support it, that over four hundred farmers had to come all the way from Saskatchewan to place their grievances before the cabinet. There has been some criticism of these people for the money which was spent to bring them here. The criticism should be directed toward the government which made it necessary to spend that money. The Prime Minister told the Saskatchewan delegation that almost all the facts which they had presented to the government had already been presented to council at some time or another. If that is so, then why did not the government do something about it? What have they been waiting for? Do they never take any steps unless they are pushed and shoved by an irate and angry public?
I warn the government that the representations made by the Saskatchewan delegation ought not to be taken lightly. They represent the point of view of a great majority of the people of that province and in fact of practically all of western Canada.
There has been some talk in the press of the possibility of the government bringing down legislation to provide ninety cents per bushel as initial payment and discontinuing the bonus. Let me say to the government, in advance, that the bulk of western farmers will not be satisfied with ninety cents. If discontinuance of the bonus is to mean discontinuance of the Prairie Farm Income bonus, there will be no objection, provided the initial price is SI per

bushel. But that is not true of the prairie farm assistance bonus, or the wheat acreage reduction bonus. These bonuses have nothing to do with the price of wheat. The prairie farm assistance bonus is to compensate a farmer for crop loss, and the wheat acreage reduction bonus is paid -to encourage the farmer not to grow wheat. Any increase in price will not remove the need for these two bonuses, and they must be continued.
Before 1 take my seat let me add this further thought. Those who listened the other evening to Mr. Evans, administrator of the A.A.A. programme in the United States, outlining the new deal that had been given to agriculture in that country during the past eight years, must have felt ashamed at the halting and feeble attempts that have been made in this country to assist agriculture. Mr. Evans told the delegates to the Canadian federation of agriculture convention about the "Food for Freedom" programme which is being put on by the American farmers. He completed his speech with a sentence which ought to be emblazoned on the walls of this chamber. He said "The American farmer is working for democracy because democracy is now working for him."
We talk often about fighting to save democracy. We cannot fight to save democracy; we can only fight for the right to practise democracy, but democracy must save itself. In the final analysis we cannot save democracy by fighting, unless democracy serves the needs of the common people. And unless the government is prepared to make democracy work for the farming and labouring population of the country, we cannot hope to get from them that enthusiasm and wholehearted cooperation without which a total war effort is impossible.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish first to congratulate the Right Hon. the Prime Minister on the magnificent personal triumph he has just obtained at the by-elections.
I have followed with close attention the discussion which has been going on ever since the opening of the session. The tone of the speeches of those who are resolved at any price to establish conscription for overseas service has in no wray surprised me. However, I view with a rather skeptical smile their claim to be serving national unity when I see them propose a measure so coercitive as to destroy the very foundations of that same national unit.
Conscription for overseas service and Canadian unity 1 Could there possibly be a greater paradox? Even before the question of conscription is submitted to the house, hon. members opposite seem to be running a marathon

The Address-Mr. Dubois
in order to see which one of them will shout quickest and loudest the "Aye, aye, ready" of the greatest blunderer Canadian public life has ever known.
I should have preferred leaving the discussion of this question to the proper time, but the opponents of national unity having thrown down the glove, there is no option but to take it up. Since they insist on talking conscription, let us talk conscription.
Conscription for what? Conscription for whom? Conscription for the benefit of what cause? The answers to these questions are to be found in agitation stirred up by the two hundred Toronto fanatics in the hire of the jackals of high finance, of the exploiters of prejudice, of the dealers in tanks and guns. For such is the infamous gang at the back of the committee of 200.
Why should we enact conscription for overseas service when we know that the voluntary system has given quite satisfactory results and that our war effort, as was stated in this house not so very long ago by the most authoritative representative of the nation chiefly interested in Canada's war effort, Right Hon. Mr. Churchill, is truly magnificent?
Does the opposition lay claim to a higher brand of patriotism than that of the Prime Minister of Great Britain? Besides, what does England ask of us? Men or equipment? Hon. members know full well that on many occasions the British government has said: We have a sufficient number of men; what we need is tools and munitions. Let us delve into the statistics regarding our war effort in terms of man-power. Canada has supplied so far:
Seamen, soldiers and airmen overseas, more than 150,000 men.
Seamen, soldiers and airmen voluntarily enlisted for service anywhere, more than
387,000	men.
Active force in Canada, more than 260,000 men.
Royal Canadian Air Force, more than 100,000 men.
Canadian navy, more than 27,000 men.
Reserve force in Canada, more than 155,000 men.
Add to that Canada's production of tools- corvettes, tanks, machine guns, munitions of all kinds, etc. etc.
Judging by the speeches of certain hon. members opposite, their plea in favour of conscription for overseas service constitutes the strongest possible argument against the conscription they demand. Let us face the facts.4
Since 1940 there have arisen a number of circumstances compelling us, if we want to be logical, to reason out the matter as follows: Either Canada is or is not likely to be attacked. If it is, common sense requires that we keep our men here to defend their own country and if Canada is not likely to be attacked, what is the sense of all our war effort?
Conscription for whom? If our country is likely to be attacked, what is the sense of the suggestion made in this house by the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Bruce) that the province of Quebec should be left in isolation? Have the hon. member's white hairs caused him, perchance, to forget the history of his adopted country? Is he not aware that if he has been able to spend happy days in Canada under the mantle of the British flag he owes it to my ancestors and to the ancestors of my French-Canadian fellow-countrymen who saved Canada for the British crown in 1776 and again in 1812? I should like to give him credit for ignorance, but his social position does not allow me to do so. It is disgraceful, Mr. Speaker, and unworthy of a man of his age to make himself the accomplice of the opponents of national unity in their endeavour to whip up the fanaticism of the committee of 200. Such despicable attempts will not scare us. Moreover, the hon. member and his friends have not had much success. Out of the 3,756,632 Canadians constituting the population of Ontario, these so-called patriots have been able to gather only 200 supporters -only 200-and that at the pric* of a heavy expenditure on the part of high finance.
My hon. leader has no need to worry. We are not afraid of that crowd. We shall in due time bring them to their sense. Should it be necessary to give them a lesson, my fellow-citizens and theirs will do so.
I have too much faith in the broadmindedness of my English-speaking fellow-citizens to believe that they will endorse a movement which aims not only at obtaining control of the government by any means, but also to stir up against each other the two great races which were already beginning to agree.
Conscription for the benefit of what cause? For the benefit of our war effort? This effort would be gravely prejudiced by recourse to compulsion. Have we not heard in this house during the present debate eminent military men state-I emphasize this point because it is also my view-that one volunteer is worth
The Address-Mr. Dubois

more than ten conscripts? And to borrow the words of my friend the hon. member for Champlain (Mr. Brunelle):
Who will believe that 50,000 more conscripts are more likely to bring victory than 120,000 volunteers at present enlisting at the rate of ten or eleven thousand a month?
No, all that is eye-wash. All that is trickery designed to cover the game of those who seek to reap large profits out of the whole business.
I have always been opposed to conscription for overseas service. I still am, and if ever the question comes before the house I will show still more convincingly, if possible, my opposition to anything of the kind.
As to the holding of the plebiscite announced in the speech from the throne, I must say that when I proposed such a measure in 1937-see Votes and Proceedings of February 9-I was far from foreseeing that it would be submitted to us in 1942. How could I vote against such a democratic measure when I proposed it myself five years ago? In conclusion, may I say, Mr. Speaker, that I am happy to associate myself under the circumstances, with the students of Laval university and with all the youth of my countiy, the group most vitally interested, and to say with them: Mr. King's government having need of us, we must give it our help. But, by the same token, we must help the government respect the pledges they have given to the people, leaving the latter free to express their views. Let us not lose our heads in the tragic hours we are going through. The tempest may rage with frightful severity during the next five or six months. Let us prepare ourselves to meet it with wisdom, firmness and courage, remembering that just as night is always followed by morning, storms are always succeeded by sunshine.
Mr. L.-PHILIPPE PICARD (Bellechasse): Mr. Speaker, it was not my intention at first to take part in this debate, but many statements by members from my province make it necessary for me to go on record and explain the position I intend to take on the address and the measure that may be introduced immediately after.
Before proceeding with my remarks it is a pleasure for me to congratulate the mover and the seconder of the address, who have so well and so eloquently discharged their duties after having both been Canadian ambassadors of goodwill to Great Britain last fall.

During these last weeks remarks have been made which might have better been left unsaid by extremists of the two schools of thought that exist on conscription. This issue has been forced on the public mind at the present time by high pressure propaganda of a financial-political group whose main enterprise fortunately flopped last Monday. It would have been preferable for the war effort of the country if it had not been used as a political weapon by the Globe-Gazette-Meighen imperialistic group. Playing with matches is a dangerous game. If it had only the effect of burning the fingers of those who hold the match, as was the case with Mr. Meighen, it would not be so bad; it might even teach a good lesson. But matches are more dangerous than that, and the fires of suspicion, fear and doubt can do more to hinder the war effort than a slowdown in the tempo of enlistment.
However, although conscription is not officially before us, everyone has talked on the matter in connection with the plebiscite referred to in the speech from the throne. It was of course to be expected that we would have an outburst of conscription fever, and I really think it has not been as bad as it might have been. The main arguments of most people who advocated conscription for overseas service failed to touch me because it overlooked for the most part Canadian interests and centred mainly on the defence of the empire and of Britain. If ever a good case could be built for conscription, it should be based upon the urgency to do it as a necessity for the defence of Canada, never on the advisability of helping Britain.
If some statements of the ultra-imperialists have annoyed me, I can say the same of some of the extreme statements of so-called nationalists of my province. Fortunately both groups received an appropriate answer last Monday from the intelligent electorate of the two largest provinces of this dominion. By their attitude since that election we can easily see how things would have become in this country had the conscriptionist press been encouraged by even a partial victory. As it is, the people of the two largest provinces have extended arms across the border to shake hands and unite in giving a vote of confidence to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) by electing the ministers he asked them to return and defeating the man who was selected by his enemies to lead a savage assault against him. No matter how the people have voted, this press is at it again. But it is not my intention to bother with them except in one case, that of an article published in the

The Address-Mr. Picard
Ottawa Citizen of yesterday, entitled "Racial Policies Cannot Prevail." The Citizen is a paper with an excellent tradition of public service to the federal capital, which made my surprise greater to find in it such an article drawing dangerous and false conclusions from the Quebec East election and the vote given to the Nationalist candidate. Would it not have been a better contribution to national unity to point out the marvellous judgment of the 16,000 Quebec electors who elected Mr. St. Laurent rather than to pretend that the 12,000 electors who supported Bouchard have all sombre designs against their fellow-Canadians? A closer study of the past elections in Quebec East would strongly invalidate the conclusions of the Citizen. In 1935 a modest Conservative lawyer of Quebec polled
10.000	votes against the Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe. These were straight party votes- Conservative votes, not Nationalist votes. In 1940, just three days before the election, the Conservative candidate-I mean the national government candidate-was withdrawn and Conservative support, in the hope of defeating Mr. Lapointe, was switched unofficially but efficiently to the Nationalist candidate, Paul Bouchard, the same man who was defeated by the present Minister of Justice; and Bouchard polled 12,000 votes against Mr. Lapointe

the same number of votes he polled against Mr. St. Laurent this week. The source of these votes is easily found by this study of previous election results-unavowed Conservative work to divide Canada and undermine confidence in the Prime Minister. Editors would render more service to the country at this time by helping to make known the accomplishments of the government rather than searching for arguments as weak as those contained in that article in order to divide Canadians one against the other.
As the questions of enlistment and mobilization have been widely discussed in this debate, Mr. Speaker, I will avail myself of the occasion to bring four suggestions to the attention of the government.
The first concerns farmers and farmers' sons. I admit readily that it would be hard to uphold that the agricultural class should benefit by special treatment that is not granted to other classes of people who do their share of war work. The primary consideration is the service rendered to the country by the land tiller and the necessity to maintain or raise the production of food in order to help feed Britain, and, above all, to maintain Canada's health and vigour by proper diets, ensured by increased supplies of food. Therefore what appears to be important is to
maintain a sufficient number of experienced men to cultivate the farm lands of the country. Although I am a layman in agriculture, I imagine it could be very easy for experts in that domain to determine how many men are needed to farm land of a definite number of acres with a given type of equipment and a certain number of head of cattle and hogs, and so on. It would be quite easy then to state that a farm of thirty acres operated with horse-drawn implements, with fifteen head of cattle, three horses and the usual small poultry yard, needs so many men. The owner, with three boys of military age, whose farm would fall under a category considered to need three men, and who is still able-bodied, would be allowed to keep two sons on the farm and would give the third to the armed services. This classification of farms could be fairly accurately established, and the decisions of boards of the war services department could then be arrived at with a maximum of security against favoritism and law-evasion.
The second point I meant to mention was the allowances granted to married men enlisting for active service overseas. At present allowances are paid to the wife and for the children uip to two. It may be that these figures were arrived at upon statistical data in an apparent scholarly way, but I cannot understand why fathers of large families are discriminated against. It surely is a much greater financial burden to raise six children than two, and it appears therefore that the father of six should in all justice receive more than the father of two. The mother of six children left behind, when the wage-earner of the family enlists, has to feed, clothe and educate six children on the same amount that is received by the mother of two. I cannot understand the justice and equity of such a decision. It is felt in the province of Quebec, where families of more than two children are the majority, that this rule is a discrimination that works against, enlistment.
Another anomaly in connection with allowances to dependents of enlisted men has been mentioned to me by one of my constituents, and I report it although I have not yet verified the fact. It is said that the mother of an enlisted unmarried man who was supporting her before his enlistment receives substantially less than does the wife of an enlisted man. If this is true I cannot understand the "what-for" of this discrimination against mothers.
Concerning also allowance to mothers, this other case came to my knowledge. In order to receive an allowance upon the enlistment of her unmarried son a mother must prove her son was supporting her before he enlisted.
The Address-Mr. Picard

There are cases when a young man of eighteen to twenty-one enlists before he ever had a chance to find employment after his coming out of school, and where the mother was painfully supporting her family by hard work. Because the son never had the opportunity to support her before his enlistment, I am told no allowance is paid to the mother.
I submit these problems to the minister and trust he will give the matter further consideration.
My fourth suggestion is to the Postmaster General (Mr. Mulock). Speaking on the address on November 21, 1940, I stated, as reported at page 328 of Hansard:
. . . that letters to members of the Canadian army should be sent free of charge, and parcels which bring cheer to a man should be sent without costs to the sender. There are many enlisted men whose families have very little personal means. While it may be fairly easy for them to send a piece of cake or some other small gift, when it comes to paying forty or fifty cents postage on a parcel it cuts into their budget quite deeply and they hesitate to send it. The man overseas wonders if his friends have forgotten him. Perhaps it could be arranged to have parcels of a certain size sent free of charge, either through the different units of the army or otherwise. If the government wants to include letters in this scheme, I am all for it. Many of these men have been away from home a long time and they deserve every encouragement they can get from those of us who are in comparative safety in this land across the sea.
I am not aware that anything of the kind has been done. I know that a bill was introduced in the United States Congress to ensure free mail to the American armed forces. I do not know what was the fate of that bill, but I imagine that something could be done here along these lines. I renew my suggestion made a year ago and I think it is just as advisable to-day.
Much has been said, Mr. Speaker, up to now about the plebiscite. I view it as a measure resulting from a desire to keep unity in the country and preserve faith in the given word. I do not think it was necessary, and I think that, had we disregarded the alarm cries of the Tories and the inspired campaign for conscription, we would have rendered a better service to the country. However, if the government consider that a release from their given pledge is going to be more conducive to public confidence in the proper carrying on of the war, the plebiscite is the only proper method for them to use. I do not personally think it necessary, as I said; but how can a man who pretends to fight for democracy and liberty object to a government using the most democratic way to make sure if the people they govern have the same views on certain aspects of the conduct of the 
war that they had two years ago? I cannot logically vote against such a measure when it is introduced in parliament. As to advice to be given the electorate I have decided to tell my constituents to vote according to their views and their conscience, and I will not attempt to influence them one way or the other.
I did not think it would be necessary, Mr. Speaker, to explain the sentiment of French Canada on conscription for service overseas, but a word from an hon. member appealing to us to abandon what was called our narrowmindedness on the question indicates there are yet people who do not fully understand our position. I will therefore try briefly to explain it.
French Canada is still and definitely opposed to compulsory service overseas, because French-Canadians are interested only in Canada and nobody has convinced them yet that compulsory service overseas is a necessity for the defence of our land. It looks too much like help to Britain and defence of the empire and too little for the defence of Canada. French-Canadians could be persuaded to accept compulsory service for overseas solely if they knew that it was the only practical way of defending their own country, and it is not an easy task to convince us of that'fact. First of all, according to me, expeditionary forces have never been, up to this war, our best and only way of defending our soil, but they have been a way of proving the solidarity of the empire; they have been the product of a patriotic urge of Anglo-Saxons exiled from their homeland but still attached to it.
Our participation in the South African war was of that nature as was, in great part, our participation in the last war. As to the present war, the situation is different: we have to cooperate with all the remaining free nations of the world in the fight to stop barbarism if we are going to survive as a nation. However, in order to do that, we must not endanger our own safety by a wrong conception of our defence problems, and I am of the opinion that there is no necessity of conscription for overseas if a proper mobilization of our human resources is made now for service in Canada, and I will refer to that in a moment.
I was explaining the French-Canadian reaction to conscription. For us there is only one country-Canada-and we do not consider that help to Britain, to maintain British trade and enlarge British benefits, as was the case in our participation in the last war, was worth the cost. French-Canadians were opposed to conscription in the last war because to them it meant only risking their lives for Britain,

The Address-Mr. Picard
for the prestige of the British empire trade in the world, and not for the safeguard of their country.
When the National Resources Mobilization Act was presented in 1940 and the principle was established that compulsory service was provided for Canada and not for participation in overseas expeditions, the vote was unanimous and the two faint murmurs of protest heard in this house had no echo in the hearts or minds of Quebec. Why was this? Because French-Canadians never objected to the defence of their country. They have proved it gallantly in the past. Some of them were even willing to help the empire; they proved it in South Africa, they proved it in 1914, and they are proving it during the present war. But as was said once by a French-Canadian leader, their participation was dictated by their mind, not by their heart.
When it comes to waging the imperial wars of Britain, or when it comes to defending Britain, we are bound to have in Canada different opinions and different viewpoints. You who were born in the British isles, as is the case with seventeen members of this house, or you who are sons of people born in the British isles, and there are fifty-three of you in the house, and all those who are more or less connected by blood to Britain, are bound to feel a call to defend your mother country, to wish to risk the ruin of your adopted country, to give everything for your mother country. It is a noble sentiment and it is bound to exist. You would not be normal if you were not stirred by these patriotic sentiments; and, mind you, I admire all those who hear the call to the defence of their mother country. But I claim that Canadians who are not of British blood who volunteer for service overseas deserve even more admiration. They deserve your gratitude and your respect because they are motivated purely by an enlarged sense of duty to Canada and by a reasoned determination to fight abroad for the preservation of the British institutions under which they have been able to develop.
A few minutes of unbiased thought, Mr. Speaker, should make people realize that men whose families have been established on the same land, or at least in the same part of the country, for from two hundred to three himdred years, are bound to have attachment to and love for their land, their country, and for no other country. They are a homogeneous group whose survival as such, and their expansion into a distinct nationality, is a miracle in itself. It has been attained by considerable sacrifice and self-denial on the part of past generations, and I am yet to find
a student of ethnology or of human geography who has not marvelled at the sturdy qualities of the French settlers and their descendants who have fought an unfavourable nature, fierce tribes of aborigines, and numerous battles, to be loyal to their flag, be it French or British. They have done all that because this land was their land and being loyal to their flag meant the defence of their country; but you must try to realize that they cannot have the same feelings of the heart for a distant land, which to most of you is the mother country, but to them is only the source of a governmental system which has given them a fair treatment when vanquished and the opportunity to wangle equality with their fellow citizens with great pains and persistence through their efforts and through their loyalty when the country was attacked.
To them, expeditions to the crown colonies will always remain imperial adventures in which their country, Canada, has no patriotic duty nor material interest; and to them expeditions across the seas will remain help to Britain and they will subscribe to it only as it remains voluntary. They would accept conscription for overseas solely if it could be proven to them that it is the only remaining way of defence of our own territoiy, and this is and will remain a most debatable question. As for myself I am as much opposed to it to-day as I have been in the past.
But, Mr. Speaker, there is something even more important to consider now than the reaction of a large part of the population of the country to conscription, and it is the study of the situation Canada faces now and how best it can cope with it.
In a world ablaze, in a universe in process of revolution, what was the position Canada could take to ensure its survival, the survival of its liberty, of all the institutions it held as sacred and precious? Could it have remained outside of the conflict, as was suggested by the member who boasted the other night that he had voted against the declaration of war? Could it have remained outside the conflict and survive? I think not. The ethnical composition of the country for one thing would have made it impossible, as two-thirds of the population would not have sat quiet and silent while the country of their fathers was in peril. But more than that, our geographical and economic position, in relation to our southern neighbour, would have made it impossible, and our position both economic and political within the commonwealth of British nations would have made it difficult. Granted, as it is by all clear-thinking citizens, that it had to enter the conflict, Canada was facing two roads to participation; entering the war as a
The Address-Mr. Picard

free nation providing first of all for its own defence, and secondly organizing ways of meeting the enemy and fighting it before it reached our shores; or entering the war as a British dominion to grant all possible help, in men, munitions and food, to the mother country, as was attempted during the last war.
My opinion is that the only way consistent with our status as defined by the act of Westminster was the first alternative. To all intents and purposes this is what has been done and the government is to be thanked for having taken the right road. But it is important to examine whether all the aspects of our war programme have been consistent with our avowed intention of waging the war for Canada and only for Canada. I think, sir, there is no harm in examining what has been done and what could be done.
I am convinced of one thing: this government has up to now done more to arm the country and gear its production for war than is realized by most of its citizens, and this splendid achievement has been reached with a minimum of inconvenience to the normal life of the country, with a wise system of economic adjustment, and while maintaining a better spirit among all citizens in the country, marred only by the alarming, politically-inspired cries of a few survivors of the Tory tribe and a few bitter, poisoned minds of the pseudonationalist clique. The government is to be given credit for this accomplishment and there should be no hesitancy in voting confidence in it on the address.
The nature and direction of our war effort has therefore to be looked into to determine whether or not it is the most consistent with our proclaimed goal-the defence of Canada. The programme outlined by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) puts all the emphasis on the expeditionary forces, and although it provides for a certain protection for the country we must candidly admit that it is not entirely adequate protection should an attack be made as was done at Pearl Harbour, for instance. I admit that at the beginning of the war the most urgent need was our participation in the resistance to the enemy far from our shores, and I approve of what was done in that regard. But is it not time to revise some of our theories in view of what is happening in a rapidly evolving war, which to-morrow may mean the invasion of Australia, because it provided too much for meeting the enemy far from its shores and not enough for meeting the enemy at home?
I may be a poor strategist, Mr. Speaker, but my contention is that the time has come to reconsider our commitments for the expedi-
tion,ary force and to look more after ourselves. A mere look at a map of the country shows that it is impossible to defend its boundaries with our present population. Taking into account our joint defence agreements with the United States, which leave our forces free for our eastern and western boundaries, we are still facing the defence of hundreds of miles of shore line on the Pacific and the Atlantic, including Newfoundland and not overlooking the valley of the St. Lawrence, the direct route to the heart of industrial Canada.
To foresee the future according to my view would mean stationing at least 100,000 men in the maritimes, 50,000 in Newfoundland.
100.000	in the provinces of Quebec and Ontario, in order that they may be easily rushed to the defence of the St. Lawrence valley, and 200,000 would not be too many for the Pacific coast. This means that the most elementary defence of the country would need a minimum of 450,000 troops.
Let us look now at our man-power. With a population of 11,500,000, Canada has about
1.102.000	unmarried men or widowers without children between the ages of 18 and 45, and
1.201.000	married men between those ages. According to the statistics of 1931 some 62 per cent of the total active male population was between these ages, and 58 per cent of the population between these ages was engaged in gainful occupations. Also about 60 per cent of the people needed in industry were between these ages, and 55 per cent of the agricultural class also fell between the ages of 18 and 45.
We can therefore take it that more than 50 per cent of that population is essentially needed for the normal life of the country. We are therefore left with 1,150,000 men, married and unmarried, between the ages of 18 and 45. From this figure ten per cent should be deducted as being the lowest number of men of military age who are at present in jobs vital to national defence, or who are neccessary to the agricultural production, to which would already have been reallotted a large number of men unfit for military service or not of .military age.
We are therefore left with a rough total of one million men. At least 25 per cent of this number are medically unfit to serve in the army. Even if a reallotment of civilian employment to citizens unfit or beyond military age could be effected with one hundred per cent success, it is highly improbable that it would leave a total available man-power for the armed services of 750,000 men.
We have already 422,000 enlisted in the three services, and the programme for 1942 outlined by the minister demands another

The Address-Mr. Picard
190.000	for overseas service, a total of
612.000	men when the programme is completed. If we carry this programme on where shall we find the men necessary for the immediate defence of the country?
My view is that our forces should be divided into two distinct categories, the Canadian territorial army and the Canadian expeditionary force. The territorial army could be mobilized through selective service under the National Resources Mobilization Act, which provides all the authority necessary to do it. This army should be trained in sufficient numbers and in the same manner as the active service force is now trained, and enough of the troops scheduled now to go abroad should be kept in Canada and assigned to this army so that the country would at all times have the necessary minimum protection.
The United States army is now spread on all the battlefields of the world, yet I doubt whether they will not keep at home enough troops for their defence. Every country should think of itself, of its own protection first, Britain did it at all times since the start of the war, and she did well. She kept a huge army at home, considering it more important-and rightly so-than to send vast armies to the other points it had to defend in order to maintain the empire intact. My contention is that Canada now should do the same.
As to the Canadian expeditionary army, it already constitutes a magnificent contribution to the fight for freedom, but should be limited in the future to a size consistent with the safety of Canada at home. Its organization should be revised so as to make it possible to reinforce, maintain and equip it while keeping a sufficient protection for the country itself.
Needless to say, the expeditionary army would be recruited, like the navy and the air force, by voluntary enlistment of civilians not yet called to the colours, and by a steady flow of volunteers from the ranks of the territorial army, which would be composed of men drafted under the selective service system. With such a balanced plan, Canada, like other belligerents, would look after its security at home while at the same time doing its share in stemming the tide of the invader on other continents.
My views may not be acceptable to the minister or his advisers, but I thought it my duty to express them to-day, encouraged as I was by the reading of British Hansard. In the British House of Commons every other day supporters of the government press forward their suggestions on the conduct of the war, which seem to be accepted in the best spirit, even if they are not always adopted.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question before he passes from that? Does he not think it would be wise to extend the provisions of the National Resources Mobilization Act so that the troops serving under that act could at least be sent to say Newfoundland, Labrador and Alaska?

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Personally I would have no objection to Newfoundland, Labrador and Alaska. I would approve of that as long as it extended to continental defence. I shall speak in a moment of a meeting I had with my own constituents at which I explained to them the same plan, and I did not hear or find many protests against that, so long as it was limited to continental hemispheric defence, which was more especially concerned with the defence of our own territory.
In conclusion, I wish to state that I shall vote for the address, because I have confidence in the Prime Minister, and I think his government deserves credit for their handling of the war effort. I might differ, as I have outlined previously, on certain methods adopted for home defence and the expeditionary force; nevertheless I consider that the government have done a splendid job and deserve approval.
As to the plebiscite, I shall approve of the measure when brought before the house, as I explained at the beginning of my remarks. And I should like, although as a newcomer in this house, I have no particular authority to do so, to make an appeal to all hon. members from my province to stand by the Prime Minister in this hour of crisis, as have stood by him the electorate of Quebec and Montreal as well as of Toronto and Welland. I am pleased to have been privileged to take part in the Quebec East by-election; it was a satisfaction to speak to crowds of serious-looking people intent on giving an intelligent verdict based on moderation and understanding and not on bigotry and prejudice. Previous to that I had invited eighty leaders from my own constituency to meet me in Quebec; one hundred and twenty came. I explained to them my attitude, told them what I have said here to-day, and I received their approval of it. Anyone would have had the same result.
I appeal to my colleagues from Quebec who might be hesitant to vote for the address. They will make no mistake in supporting the Prime Minister and the government. Let not the splendid lesson in national unity given this week by Ontario and Quebec go unheeded. The results of the four by-elections were the fruit of tolerance. Tolerance, the hope of the
The Address-Mr. Slaght

world, may yet save Canada. Let us all work to that end, in the same spirit of cooperation for victory.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, permit me first to congratulate my good friends the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Fournier), the hon. member for Brantford City (Mr. Macdonald), the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) and the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore), upon their very fine contributions to this debate. The excellence of their addresses was not a surprise to me, because I was privileged to travel with them for a month throughout the mother country, where they presented Canada's position to the people of the motherland in a way creditable indeed. I endorse to the full, in order to save time and not repeat it in detail, what was so well put by the hon. member for Lethbridge with reference to the friendship engendered among all six of us on our English trip, and also his tribute to the devotion and hospitality of our hosts over there and the thoughtfulness of those on this side of the water who made our trip possible.
Much has already been said in this house by my associates in that journey, about the trip itself, so I shall content myself with looking forward to making addresses throughout the country, as I have already done in part, in order that those not so fortunate as we were may better understand the devastation, the sorrow and the destruction which we found; but also, transcending all that, the quiet, grim determination of the British people in all walks of life to see this war through to final victory. We did not confine our visit to the well-to-do people or the white-collar folk. We went down into the holds of ships; we went through the dockyards; we saw the trawler men; we talked with people at work at their machines in the munition factories, to farmers tilling the soil and to our own soldiers and airmen, in order that we might learn at first hand the very innermost life of the British people. From the humblest, battered home right through the picture to Buckingham Palace we as Canadians were received with the utmost cordiality and friendship. At the many places we visited and the many receptions, luncheons and dinners we enjoyed, people who previously had been strangers to us were eager to listen to the story of our Canadian war effort, and in every case seemed reluctant to let us go on our way. Let me conclude this reference by saying to you, Mr. Speaker, that everywhere we went, the British people were happy and contented with Canada and Canada's war effort, and they marvelled that we had been able to do so much.

Let me now turn to a consideration of the speech from the throne, and first I desire to utter a friendly word to my friends from the province of Quebec. Personally I have a great regard for the province of Quebec and its people. I number among my warmest and most cherished friends Canadians of French descent both within and without this House of Commons. I have the most abiding faith in their loyalty to the British empire, and there is still fresh in my mind a picture of the devastated homes of old France, of the sufferings, the sacrifices and the magnificent contributions made by that country, now suffering under the cruel heel of a conquering enemy, side by side with us in the last great war. To those of my friends from Quebec who entertain genuine doubts as to the wisdom of the course being pursued by this government, let me point out in the most friendly spirit that we must be free to adopt whatever course the welfare of our country demands, whether it be compulsory service for overseas or whether voluntary enlistment should prove fully to meet the needs. I appeal to them for their support for this plebiscite; for their continuing contribution, as in the past, to the various armed forces of this country, in order to throw back into their teeth the words of those hot-headed, uncharitable people who may by evil or insulting speeches impugn the loyalty of the great French-Canadian race to the British empire.
Never was there a time in history when the people of that great race, by their conduct toward this plebiscite, by their continuing voluntary enlistment, have had such a splendid opportunity to prove once and for all that this country is united and will go through to victory as a powerful national unit, in order that we may take our place at the peace table and make our voice heard in the final declarations that will settle the future happiness of the civilized world. Nor does the disturbance last night in Montreal, referred to in the press to-day, much as it is to be regretted, indicate to me anything more than that a small, misguided group of youths, stirred up by inflammatory doctrine, saw fit for the moment to carry on unseemly demonstrations. Let us not forget that when the Duplessis government of Quebec went to the people, there was much more noise of a disruptive character than occurred last night. At that time the great French-Canadian people had their opportunity to weigh the effort that was made to take them away from their loyalty to Britain; and after that misguided campaign, to use a mild expression, they gave an overwhelming answer to those who desired

The Address-Mr. Slaght
to take them down a path that could only-lead ultimately to the destruction of the unity of this country.
Before I deal with the plebiscite, Mr. Speaker, permit me to make a personal statement as to my conception of my duty in connection -with this war. I will take from no man any imputation that I have not always striven to place our country at the side of the motherland and to take the most effective possible measures to defeat our enemies and make victory sure. On March 24, 1938, I begged this House of Commons to double the estimates for the air service in Canada. I urged the house to set up training schools across Canada, at Halifax, Quebec, Montreal, the Royal Military College at Kingston, Toronto, Winnipeg, Calgary, Regina, Vancouver and Victoria, to turn out 8,000 well trained men, consisting of one thousand piiots who would be capable of operating the highest speed machines, with seven thousand mechanics on the ground to service them. I told the house on that occasion we would have
8.000	men who, in my humble judgment, would be of as great value in war time as
200.000	men would be, enlisted in the other branches of the service, and who would make a greater contribution to empire war service and to empire defence. Not a word of encouragement or approval for such a course did I obtain from any of my hon. friends sitting across from me, or, in fact, from any of the members of the house.
The following session, on May 13, 1939-and note the date-for which year the estimates for the air service had been notably increased, being brought down at $29,000,000, I again urged the house to double that year's appropriation, repeated my plea of the year before, and again urged for its support grounds which I have just detailed to hon. members.
On that occasion, I made a statement relative to the use those 8,000 trained airmen would be. My statement is found at page 4041 of Hansard as follows:
I have verified this by conversation with one of the greatest airmen of the world, a distinguished Canadian. . . .
I had had the privilege of doing that, before speaking. The statement I verified was that
8.000	trained airmen, 1,000 of whom would be pilots, would be as great a contribution to defence as 200,000 men in the other forces.
Not a word of support on that occasion. Let me be fair to the then Minister of National Defence, the present Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie). On both occasions before speaking I secured his approval for my urging upon the house the adoption of this proposal. If
it had been adopted, what untold value such a force might have been at Dunkirk, or at Hong Kong, or to-day at Singapore, or to-morrow in British Columbia.
I do not wish to be misunderstood in recalling my plea of 1938 and 1939 when I got no response from the house. I felt strongly on the subject. I could have followed it up in the country with speeches on public platforms. I did not do so. Therefore I am as much to be indicted as any other hon. member for not having followed up what seemed to me something we should then do, and something which involved the youth of our land going across and fighting in the British channel in defence of the motherland. Therefore there is no question about it, so far as I am concerned, that I approved meeting the enemy anywhere he might be found.
There recently appeared on the horizon a new leader for the great Conservative party. When he appeared on the horizon, when some by-elections were in sight, with the possible exception of that caused by the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Bruce) who, I am sorry, is not at the moment in his seat-he is a friend of mine, and one for whom I have high regard -there was no pother or stir about the question of conscription or compulsory service for overseas. In the house and in the country we had travelled down the road of preparation. Canada was making a splendid contribution, with not only national unity and cooperation up to that time among various peoples of different racial origin throughout the country, but also real and honest cooperation among the various parties and groups in the house who, in the main, have all directed their efforts toward a united front in the prosecution of the war.
Speaking only for myself-and I want to be the one to say this-I think it is time in the debate to pay tribute to the leader of the official Conservative opposition (Mr. Hanson), and to his group in the house; also to the leaders of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation and Social Credit groups, whose friendship I cherish, and have had the privilege of developing in an intimate way in the past few months.
Nor would it be fair for me to close my speech without reference to the Hon. R. J. Manion who, during part of the war period, led his party in the house, who, since, has followed and is still following the splendid example set by Wendell Willkie in the United States, and who under this government is now conducting a most important an onerous war task, as director of the A.R.P. activities throughout Canada. I am told he is doing an extremely good job of it.
The Address-Mr. Slaght

I say this, not because we have not had differences, and sometimes a bit of heat across the floor of the chamber-and not only across the floor of the chamber, but some fairly warm blasts and counterblasts passing up and down the side-lines on, the other side of the chamber among men who differ from each other on various points. But the point I emphasize right now-and I am glad to do it-is that all groups in the house have cooperated splendidly for the common purpose. What I want to deprecate is that, fanned up by partisan influence, by expletive, high-powered adjectives and denunciation, a little group of high-powered politicians outside the house have picked this time, on the eve of our new victory loan, to try to tear the country wide apart, w'hen there is no need in the world to do so.
A number of people in Canada are in favour of compulsory service for overseas, beginning right now. Many hold to the honest opinion that conditions have changed, that they have become more serious, and that the need for increased man-power has brought us to the place where, in their view, voluntary enlistment has perhaps begun to lag a little, and the other system should be adopted. But do not let us forget that right down to a month ago, when this new politician appeared on the scene and stirred the kettle with inflammatory attacks upon the government-a government by the way which had graciously refused to oppose him in York South-down to that time, I say, practically everybody in Canada had endorsed and approved the system of voluntary enlistment, a system which is now so viciously attacked by those who heretofore voted for and supported it.
My hon. friends of the Conservative party across the floor, with the single exception of the leader of the opposition and the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church), of whom I am not sure-and I stand corrected if in any way I am in error-all came into the house and were elected under the banner of the Hon. R. J. Manion in March, 1940, and all adopted Mr. Manion's platform, the man who was their leader, in calling for a so-called national government. They worked for him and he worked for them, and they were elected under that banner.
Let me place on Hansard what their leader on their behalf and for himself pledged the' people of Canada on March 4, 1940. Two weeks before polling he issued a press release, only two paragraphs of which I shall place on record:
Conscription to my mind was a failure in the last war, as it raised only about 10,000 men out of more than 500,000, and it stirred up much misunderstanding in our country. For 
that reason and because conscription is not necessary in this war, and because as I have said on other occasions, it is the duty of a public man to hold Canada together as a nation, I am absolutely opposed to conscription.
My hon. friends opposite-and if I am not right, let them stand up and say so-adopted the policy of this Conservative leader, as enunciated to the people. They went to their constituencies and made speeches, tacitly relying, at all events, on the platform he was putting forward, and owing their seats in the house to-day to that kind of pledge.
But that is not all. I have a word for my hon. friends of the two other parties. The leader of the Social Credit party, (Mr. Blaekmore), a good friend of mine, said this on May 26:
The Liberal party obtained the mandate of the people in the last election while opposing the conscription of man-power. It is clear therefore that the question of conscription is a dead issue in Canada until another mandate is given by the people at a new election.
My hon. friend always stands by his word.
The leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party, (Mr. Coldwell)-I am sorry he is not in his seat at the moment, -as reported in the Globe of March 14, reiterated his party's unalterable opposition to conscription, and I think my hon. friends will feel that I am fair when I say that that was their policy in the last election. It is small wonder that we do not hear Doctor Manion's voice supporting his party in this campaign. He believes in the Willkie way of doing things. That is why every place you turn, Mr. Speaker, you get right back to the one man who has stirred up this whole agitation, the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, the man who prided himself for years as one of the leaders of a party whose slogan was, "No truck or trade with the Yankees." That was emblazoned on banners above his platform at his political meetings. He is the same man who accepted from former Prime Minister Bennett a seat in that other place and supported Mr. Bennett in his campaign to blast Canada's way into the markets of the United States and of the world. Are the people of Canada to trade our magnificent Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) who is the leader of this country to-day, for this "no truck or trade" politician and this "blaster" fellow? Is he the right man to place at the head of this country when we have just concluded a treaty with the United States for the mutual defence of North America, and when we have sitting to-day a joint commission for the greater protection of North America, and have established the most friendly relations between Canada and the United States that have ever existed since

The Address-Mr. Slaght
confederation? Is he the type of man to lead Canada through a war when only within the last few weeks the United States have said to us, "We will give you equal priorities with us on our steel. We have got our arms around your shoulders. We want your nickel in return for some of the things you want, but we will go hand in hand with you from now on." Could they entirely forget that he affronted them a few short years ago with the most insulting slogan that ever man tried to ride into office on-"no truck or trade with the Yankees"? Over there, "Yankee" is a word that is used only when somebody tries to insult someone. He is the leader you are asked to place in power as against the present Prime Minister, who has devoted at least the last five years of his life most faithfully and earnestly to cultivating, fostering and cementing the most friendly feelings and relations not only between Canada and the United States but also between Great Britain and the United States. This man has lived to see his dream come true, and is he to be rewarded with vilification and abuse because, instead of breaking his word to the people as these outside Tories would have him do, he proposes to ask the people to relieve him from the solemn pledge he gave and which every other member of this House of Commons on both sides of the house gave to their people either by implication or directly?
What is all this bother about? Stripped of its political trappings and torn from its coating of hypocrisy, it all boils down to a denunciation of the government because they want to permit the people of Canada to give them a free hand to enact whatever measures they may deem to be best in the interests of this country.
I was glad to hear my hon. friend the member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas), with whom I am not always in accord, state that he believes the proper form of government was, when a pledge had been given, to consult the people on the great issues before forcing something to the contrary down their throats.
Let me quote an authority that I commend to my hon. friends of the French-Canadian race. In 1917 our great and departed leader, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, after the Right Hon. Sir Robert Borden, who was then leading the government, had proposed a measure of compulsory service overseas without consulting the people in any way, begged Sir Robert not to ram this measure down the throats of the people of Canada but to consult them in a referendum, and this is the language he used on that occasion, which will be found at page 2403 of Hansard of June 18, 1917:
What I propose is that we should have a referendum and a consultation of the people
upon this question. I have taken the referendum, not that I have been very favourable towards it, but I find that the idea of the referendum has made enormous progress in Canada, and that it has been adopted by the political associations in the western provinces as a method of political action.
My hon. friends from the west will be prepared to bear out the statement of those early days. Sir Wilfrid goes on:
If we are to have peace, if there is to be unity, we must meet the wishes of the labouring classes, who have asked for this privilege. When the consultation with the people has been had, when the verdict has been pronounced, I pledge my word, my reputation that to the verdict, such as it is, every man will submit, and I claim to speak at least so far as is concerned the province from which I come.
I commend to my French-Canadian fellow members as they pass that great statue standing in our grounds, in this noble enclosure on parliament hill, to remember at least those words of their great leader; and, following them, they cannot go far astray.
Two main points have been advanced against the taking of the plebiscite. First, that it will cost some money, estimated, I think properly, at about one and a half million dollars-out of a total annual expenditure of three billion dollars. Is it worth a million and a half dollars to have a government which has kept its word-instead of breaking it? Is it worth a million and a half dollars and sixty or seventy days of time to have a government carry on the business of the country in war time which cannot be pointed at with an accusing finger and told by the people of the country, "Your word is no good. You have breached your trust to me." I am going to watch with interest if and when my hon. friends of the Conservative party rise and bow to a negation of this plebiscite because if they do, and vote against it, who that listened to their pledges of that day can not but come and say, "You are a liar?" And what will their answer be? "Oh, well, but, my dear friend, times have changed." Let my hon. friends take that course if they see fit. They are only-I do not hold this against them-a small item in this House of Commons proportionately. But I do not want the government, the great Liberal party in this house, to have to sit with a blush of shame on their cheeks when any of their constituents who heard them make that pledge come forward and say, "You are a liar." And that is what they can do unless this simple, honourable course of consulting the people is taken.
Does any honest man-I put it that way because this is one of the arguments we have heard used, although I do not think it has been used in this chamber; I have unfor-
The Address-Mr. Slaght

tunately not been here all the time-does any honest man say that those reinforcements now under arms in Canada in the active service army who have volunteered to go overseas if we want to send them, the 120,000 of them now in uniform, are not sufficient to replace even the most dire casualties which might occur in our overseas army of 130,000 men? That is sheer political bunk, fed to the people to inflame them. That sort of inflammatory, false argument is whipped up to try to create political prejudice against this government in the minds of those splendid people-fathers, mothers, wives and sisters-who have menfolk in the army overseas. This whole move is largely an effort to defeat our Prime Minister. It is directed to him by some gentlemen who want to get rid of him. I am glad to see that the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Bruce) has returned to his seat. Not long ago I paid him a personal tribute which I desire to repeat in his presence; he has not had, perhaps, many friends politically.
We know what the Eight Hon. Arthur Meighen thinks and says about the Prime Minister of Canada. We know also the views of a little group of other gentlemen. I am going to put on Hansard the opinions of some men who are not interested in playing politics in Canada. The first one to whom I refer is the Right Hon. Winston Spencer Churchill, who on September 4, 1941, said, in London, with regard to our war effort:
The war effort of Canada is immense in ships, aircraft, air training, in finance and in food, and constitutes an element in the resistance of the British empire without which that resistance could not be successfully maintained.
Then, speaking to the distinguished gathering which had cheered our leader's outstanding address in the Guildhall a few months before, Mr. Churchill said of our Canadian war Prime Minister:
To-day you have listened to a memorable and momentous declaration made here amid our ruins of London. You have listened to a speech which, I think, all those who have heard it will feel, explains the long-continued authority which -Mr. Mackenzie King has wielded when, during more than fifteen years, he has been Prime Minister of Canada.
Then this further tribute: Mr. Churchill said, with regard to our Prime Minister:
You have a great knowledge of the flexible organization, a system ever changing and ex-paneling, yet ever growing into a greater harmony, by which the British commonwealth of nations is conducted.
You have also knowledge of your own people and your association with them is so long and so intimate it has enabled you to realize and express in these hours of trouble a more complete unity of Canada than has ever before been achieved.
[Mr. Slaght.1
If you were jurors on a lawsuit, would you prefer the evidence of Arthur Meighen or the evidence of Winston Churchill?

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The smashing of windows in Montreal does not look very much like unity.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Well, without being unfair to the hon. member, that is the sort of talk which, if it is indulged in on the floor of this house, will tear this country limb from limb. Did my hon. friend hear the Duplessis talk from Quebec for a time, and does he not remember that, with the aid of the leaders of the government of this house, and the sound, sane thinking people of Quebec, Duplessis was snowed under and disgraced by the vote of the overwhelming majority of the people of that province?
Just one more tribute from Mr. Winston Churchill, and this, remember, after he and the great president of the United States had met upon a vessel in the Atlantic ocean. He said:
Canada, with those relations of friendly, affectionate intimacy with the United States on the one hand and with her unswerving fidelity to the British commonwealth and motherland on the other is the link which joins together these great branches of the human family. In Mr. King we have a Canadian statesman who always has preserved the most intimate relations with the great republic of the United States and whose name and voice are honoured there as they are on this side of the Atlantic.
I had an opportunity of meeting the president of the United States a few weeks ago and I know from him of the great esteem in which Mr. Mackenzie King is held and how much he has contributed to joining together in close, sympathetic action, the republic of the United States and the Dominion of Canada. Canada is the linchpin of the English-speaking world.
What does General McNaughton say, that man for whom I fancy every hon. member has the greatest and highest esteem and regard? What did he say in his message to the Canadian troops at Christmas time? It has already been put upon Hansard, of February 5. 1942, at page 346, and I shall not read it all, but I shall just quote that passage wherein he says:
From a very small beginning the Canadian army has now grown to many tens of thousands of men and women. New units and formations and reserves have come to us as quickly as ships could be found to bring them here, and as they have arrived the organization of our military headquarters, reinforcement units, hospitals, schools, repair establishments and many other needed facilities have been pressed forward; . . .
Throughout this long period of preparation which circumstances have given us, the corps, divisions, armoured formations and other field units have been completed in equipment, and trained together and with squadrons of the Royal Canadian Air Force assigned to army cooperation.

The Address-Mr. Slaght
That is the tribute. Is it false or is it true? Who will stand up and gainsay the language of General McNaughton? Yet, by implication, a great many of those who have denounced the war effort of this government are doing just that thing.
Let me appeal to my hon. friends opposite. I suppose it is too much to expect that they would drop their amendment and let this house get on as a unit. Let us have this plebiscite; let us bring in the bill next week or as fast as possible, put it through, and take the plebiscite. I have the greatest faith that every province in this dominion, when that plebiscite is taken, will entrust this government with continued control of the Canadian war effort.
One point which has been advanced against the plebiscite by a great many, including I believe Mr. Drew-I am not sure whether any hon. member has raised it-is, "If you hold a plebiscite, what will they say of us in the United States? Oh, that will be terrible! What will they have to say of us?"

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Let us vote on this question this afternoon.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: What did the hon. member say?

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I said, about your question of withdrawing the amendment, why not call a vote right now, and get along with the business of the house?
