speechtext:
I commend the hon. member for that; he is a splendid adherent to the cause. Let my friends who feel that way about the United States console themselves with this. The New York Times is admittedly the greatest friend of Britain so far as daily newspapers across the border are concerned, and it stands almost in a class by itself. This is what that great organ, expressing public opinion in that great republic, has to say. On January 26 the Times said editorially:
. .	. that when opponents of conscription in
Canada assert that the forthcoming plebiscite will throw doubt upon the dominion's "exertion of her full power" in the war, "her friends- and we are all her friends-must protest."
That is what our friends in the United States are protesting-the statements made by the opponents of this plebiscite.
There is one matter to which I should like to turn for a moment if I may be allowed to
do so. It has nothing to do with the plebiscite, but to me it is important. I refer to the question of our introducing as rapidly as possible a system of parliamentary secretaryships. The house may recall-and this is nonpolitical, I am sure-that in the speech from the throne in 1936 there appeared this clause, that there would be brought in a bill to provide for the creation of parliamentary secretaryships. I had the honour to move the address in reply on that occasion, and I used in Hansard certain language in which I commended the idea. I suppose most young speakers commend the speech from the throne, and I did so on that occasion, giving the reasons therefor. This is what I said on that occasion-I hope hon. members will bear with me because the matter is, in my judgment, ten times more important now than it was at that time-and I commend it to the consideration of the Prime Minister and of the government. I said, as reported at page 31 of Hansard of 1936:
Then we find a proposal to create parliamentary secretaryships, and this proposal will, I hope, meet with the approval of every hon. member of this house. It is established in the mother of parliaments, and I believe is fully approved by British statesmen regardless of party affiliations. It should create the building up in this house of a body of men who because of the experience gained as under-secretaries will be better able in the future to carry on the responsible duties attaching to cabinet positions. I fancy that the right hon. leader of the opposition and some of those *who sit beside him will agree with me that it will afford a measure of relief to the ministers of the day who can very properly turn over some of the exacting details of their offices to undersecretaries, and do so without impairing the efficiency of their work. From every viewpoint I submit to the house that this administrative reform is one that will be found of benefit to Canada.
My recent visit to England has confirmed me tenfold in that view, and I will mention one incident. We were privileged to visit eleven cabinet ministers, including every member of the war cabinet, for half an hour privately in their rooms. I was in Mr. Herbert Morrison's room, and there was with him, a young gentleman, a member of the house, whom he introduced as his parliamentary secretary. Mr. Morrison turned to him at times for verification of certain figures, and this young gentleman was very helpful. I said to Mr. Morrison, "I don't suppose you could carry on without your parliamentary secretary." He answered, "Carry on? I could not possibly. I have three parliamentary secretaries, and with them I find it difficult to dc all the work I have to do." And why not? There is plenty of material in this house. There are eighteen members of this house whom I
The Address-Mr. Slaght

could mention. Of course, I have not the privilege of picking either cabinet associates or parliamentary secretaries. I am putting this on Hansard merely as a recommendation to my right hon. friend the Prime Minister. Let me run over the list as rapidly as possible. There are the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Bra-dette), the hon. member for Renfrew South (Mr. McCann), the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. McNiven), the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Roebuck), the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross), the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Edwards), the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. McKinnon), the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith), the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid). Those bagpipes would, I am sure, give an extra swirl if we had the hon. member for New Westminster as a parliamentary secretary. Then there is a wealth of material from Quebec-

There is the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis). Where is he now? That is my view of the war. I speak for myself alone, but I commend this idea to the government of the day.
One word more if I have time. I wish to say something about British Columbia, and I am sorry that the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) is not at the moment in his seat. May I refer to British Columbia and the Japanese situation and the fifth column in that province?

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Go on.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I will be brief. The fifth-column question, the matter of internment, is one to which I have devoted myself particularly for the last two years, under the guidance of, in cooperation with, and at the request of the late lamented Minister of Justice, to whose memory I pay great tribute to-day. I know something about this matter. I went to British Columbia at my own expense a year ago to look into the Japanese question, and I say this to the Minister of National Defence: Get those interned Japs across the mountains out of British Columbia without any more delay. You cannot move too fast. Three days from now you may be too late.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: One day.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Well, one day, if you like. But let us have it done. Someone says, "But where will you house them?" Well, two or three contractors from Calgary or Edmonton could put up temporary housing for 1,500 or
2,000	men in two or three weeks' time, and they could be taken care of, fed, guarded and protected.
One word more and I close. I am on the indulgence of the house. To what was the downfall of Norway due? The Quislings within. When did she learn of that danger? Not until the hun was over the border into Norway and the traitors cropped up like mushrooms overnight. To what was the downfall of France, Belgium, Holland due? The cream of the British army, 350.000 men, found that Hitler had whipped eight million men in thirty-three days. Why? Because of enemy treachery from within. There is no question about that. Now then, do not let us wait. We have the machinery; we have

The Address-Mr. Parent
them picked up in the area proclaimed to be a war area; let us get them out of that province before irreparable damage may be done. I offer that as my view, from one who thinks he knows something about the matter, to my hon. friend the Minister of National Defence.
In our present dilemma, which is indeed grave-and we await news that may be yet more so-my word to this house, and a word which I believe can govern the attitude of any man who wants us to give an all-out effort to win this war, is this-I use the language of Mr. Churchill.
We have great reason for vigilance and concern, hut no room for despair.
Mr. CHARLES PARENT (Quebec West and South) (Translation); Mr. Speaker, since the opening of this debate a considerable degree of unrest has been noticeable on all sides. The intemperate language used by some hon. members shows that the war of nerves started by the Toronto committee of 200 has reached us.
Be assured, Mr. Speaker, that in submitting my reasons for voting against the address and the proposed plebiscite I shall be brief and moderate.
The discussion so far has revealed the existence in this house of four distinct schools of thought. This shows how difficult it is to appraise the government's attitude and to make it acceptable to the various groups.
The first school of thought endorses the government's war policy such as it was originally, that is, free, voluntary and moderate, the result of a compromise due to the firm attitude of the Quebec leaders. This school, by its support of the proposed plebiscite, is taking an alarming turn towards what may become to-morrow a coercive, nonvoluntary and immoderate war policy.
Many hon. members, I know, are supporting the plebiscite while reserving the right to vote against the conscription bill when it comes before the house. It is my view, Mr. Speaker, that once freed from its pledges the government will not have to bring in a conscription bill, as it already has all the power required to achieve this end. I do not object to the principle of a plebiscite, but I maintain that the government has no right to use such a measure for the purpose of allowing the majority to repudiate sacred pledges given to a minority.
The second school of thought is that of the Toiy element. After hearing the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson), one can say with Abraham: "It is the hand of Esau, but the voice of Jacob." The Toronto committee of 200 has voiced its demand for a total effort with conscription, but not conscription of
wealth, for that would too seriously affect their bank accounts.
It is scarcely necessary to say that I intend to vote against the amendment proposed by the leader of the opposition.
The third school of thought is led by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). I must admit that the hon. gentleman has shown a praiseworthy consistency, since he preaches in 1942 what he preached in 1939. He advocates a total war effort with conscription of man-power, of industry, of resources and of wealth. I must regretfully say, however, that I do not share his views and that I shall vote against the amendment to the amendment.
The fourth school has no leader, but it has an ideal-a Canadian ideal. We acknowledge that we have certain duties and certain obligations towards England, but within reasonable limits and in proportion to our means. We recognize that our only country is Canada and that it is Canada that we must defend and that we are ready to defend. This school of thought has endorsed without recrimination Canada's war effort which was to be free, voluntary and moderate. It has accepted every compromise for the sake of national unity, but to-day it refuses to go a step farther, for fear of prejudicing this same national unity. Solemn pledges were given to the electors at the 1940 general election. Whatever the cost, we insist on respecting these pledges.
That school of thought is of the opinion that the government can no more release themselves of their undertaking through a plebiscite than could ten endorsers relieve themselves from any obligation to pay a note through voting one and all against their creditor. Let us remember that this compromise was agreed upon by the province of Quebec on the [DOT] one hand and by all the provinces of Canada on the other. Quebec alone could renounce its vested rights.
If I now take the responsibility of voting against the address and the proposed plebiscite, it is that I am determined to honour my undertaking and because I believe this plebiscite will constitute a dangerous precedent, for, by this measure the government is taking a great step towards conscription for overseas service.
Lapointe possessed great parliamentary experience, a deep understanding of law and a knowledge of the meaning and implications of words. Never did he leave any door open, however, in his statements on conscription. He had been in the house with Laurier in 1917. He had approved Laurier on the referendum. But the experience of 1917 had taught him a lesson. He was acquainted with all
The Address-Mr. Parent

democratic methods of consulting the people. Nevertheless, in making his statement on conscription Lapointe always burnt his bridges behind him. He consented every sacrifice, but would not leave the weapon of the plebiscite in the hands of the majority to overcome the minority.
Lapointe never said: "I will never agree to conscription until it has been voted by the people through a plebiscite or referendum". He quite positively and definitely stated: "I shall never accept conscription nor will I *remain a member of a government which would enforce it". As the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Lacroix) so aptly recalled, Lapointe said: "Never".

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: On June 18th, 1940, he stated before the whole country that the province of Quebec opposed compulsory' service for overseas, that he would oppose such a *measure and that were it suggested by the government he would cease to be a member of such government. Lapointe's undertakings as regards conscription for overseas service constitute his political will. Let us respect it.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
It has been said, Mr. Speaker, that Quebec is opposed to conscription for overseas service. That is true. We have a great many reasons for opposing it. In order to understand such an attitude one must be acquainted with Quebec's soul. Its state of mind, its character and its education are the result of three centuries of struggle, resolute labour, steadfastness and faith in its mission.
How truly has the author of "Maria Chap-delaine" said:
We came here three centuries ago and we have remained. Those who brought us here could return among us without bitterness or sorrow, for while it is true that we have not learned much, we have certainly forgotten nothing. We brought from overseas our prayers and our songs; they have remained ever the same. We have brought within our breasts our countrymen's hearts, valiant and vivacious, as open to pity as to mirth, the most human of all human hearts. Our creed, our language, our virtues and even our failings become sacred, intangible things, and will remain so to the end.
The province of Quebec does not forget that it has nearly 2,700,000 French Canadians as compared with about 650,000 people of all other extractions. Nor does it forget that the average Quebec family has four children against less than two in the other provinces. Owing to that very fact, conscription would mean to Quebec a sacrifice proportionately far greater than to the other provinces.

The province of Quebec does not forget either that taxes fall more heavily upon its families, that in the economic, financial and administrative fields, it has had to overcome formidable handicaps in order to survive, and that conscription would mean the upsetting of its entire economy.
It would be a mistake to believe that our national life draws its sole inspiration from France. Most French Canadian families can trace back their ancestors over a period of one, two or three centuries, and I do not think there are to-day one hundred French Canadian families with relatives in France. Such a fact makes it clear that Canada is the French Canadians' home land and that Quebec especially represents for them the result of labour, accomplished by many generations, that they are determined to live and die there but, above all, they are ready to defend the Canadian soil against anyone who might attempt to conquer it.
I can conceive that such a state of mind is bard to understand for some of our Englishspeaking fellow citizens who live in Canada but whose minds and hearts are in England. We do not have among our people a Lord Beaverbrook, a Viscount Bennett, a Beverley Baxter or a George W. Weston. Those men after acquiring wealth in Canada have left our shores to spend their declining years in England.
The province of Quebec does not forget either that it enjoys a certain measure of freedom, but it is well enough acquainted with history to know that whatever it enjoys was only obtained after hard struggles and that, besides, it is not the debtor but rather the creditor of Britain.
It is all too frequently forgotten how generous and loyal Quebec was in 1775, 1812 and 1914. Vimy, Courcelette, Ypres, Passchen-daele give striking evidence that after the lapse of one hundred years, we have fully preserved the virtues and gallantry of our fathers.
The province of Quebec also remembers the days of 1917 and better propaganda than is now going on will have to be used if our young men are to be brought to believe that Canada's first defence line is in England.
I represent a constituency in the city of Quebec where decent and peaceful citizens were killed during the 1917 troubles, and my electors knew when they gave me their confidence in 1940, that I would honour my pledges and protect their interests.
Mr. Speaker, these are a few of the reasons why Quebec is opposed to conscription for overseas service; many others could be enu-

The Address-Mr. Emmerson
merated but there is no point in taking up the time of the house. I have mentioned enough to justify my vote against the address and the plebiscite.
Yes, Mr. Speaker, the province of Quebec is opposed to conscription for overseas service, but it is not opposed to the war effort through voluntary enlistment. Religious and civil authorities have been generous in their support of the Canadian war effort, but the Government have enlisted this loyal support by committing themselves not to resort to conscription for overseas service. Let us keep our word.
From certain quarters, we hear that these pledges were made by the leaders and the members under circumstances different from those which presently obtain. In 1939, 1940 and 1941, the Rome-Berlin-Tokio axis was already in existence and our leaders knew full well that Great Britain could not rely on her allies of 1914.
Furthermore, Germany had exhibited the might of its military machine to the world, by cutting to pieces, in a few weeks, the gallant Polish armies. The Canadian leaders were conversant or should have been with the deficiencies of the allied armies and it was easy to gauge the situation in comparing the events of 1917 with those of 1940. However, in spite of all this, while Hitler was marching through Europe, we were told time and again that conscription for overseas service would never be resorted to. We even denounced as evil-minded citizens those who questioned the word of our leaders, the word of honest citizens, by their reminder that other leaders, Borden, in Canada, Chamberlain in England, had to go back on their word against conscription.
For the last thirty years, we have campaigned against conscription for overseas service and the Quebec population had good reason to believe that their attitude in this matter was just as reasonable as that of Australia where there are no French Canadians.
All this goes to prove that Quebec is now influenced by its education, its formation and its sense of duty toward threatened Canada.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, allow me to render homage to the heroes of Hong Kong and especially to the Royal Rifles of Canada, of Quebec City, and offer the tribute of my sincerest admiration and deepest sympathy to their bereaved families. Though unfortunate, this expedition has been glorious. Those sons of Canada have given living testimony to the gallantry and courage of the Canadian soldier. It has been suggested that Hong
Kong should be-forgotten. For my part, I say, in the words of Gambetta: "Let us always think, but never talk, about it."
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I proceed with the remarks I have to make with respect to the subject matter of this debate, may I be permitted to offer my congratulations to the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Fournier) who had the honour of moving the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Both in manner of delivery and in thoughts expressed his speech was worthy of the highest praise. It warmed my heart, as I know it did the hearts of all hon. members listening to his words of commendation, inspired by his association with the men and women of Great Britain. I wish also to offer my congratulations to the hon. member for Brantford City (Mr. Macdonald) who, like the hon. member for Hull, had an opportunity to visit the old country quite recently and see first hand the effects of the blitz from the centre of our empire, and had the privilege of mingling and talking with those who had suffered so severely, and who are still carrying on so magnificently.
While perhaps some may consider that the present debate has gone far enough, and are impatient to get on with the job of pushing forward the war effort, I believe I owe it to the people of my constituency of Westmorland to say a few words, as their representative in the House of Commons. Westmorland is a large constituency, and has the second largest population among the constituencies of New Brunswick. I am proud of my county because of what it has done in peace time, and prouder still because of what it is doing in the present war. We are a truly Canadian section of the dominion, with a mixture of English, Irish, Scotch and French. Approximately two-thirds of the citizens are Englishspeaking, and the remaining third are Frenchspeaking. There is no more loyal part of our country than Westmorland, whose chief centre is the city of Moncton, often called the hub of the maritimes. Westmorland is the core of the maritimes, and what more loyal part of the dominion is there than the maritime provinces?
If we may judge loyalty by enlistments, then Moncton, Westmorland county and all the maritimes will certainly not take second place to any other part of Canada. We have

The Address-Mr. Emmerson
had our share of losses, too, on land, on sea and in the air. May I be pardoned for calling attention to the fact that the glorious role played by the Royal Irish Rifles of Quebec at Hong Kong fills us with pride; for on the nominal roll of that great battalion were the names of over 450 men from the maritime provinces, French, English, Irish and Scotch.
I desire now to pay my tribute to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), my honoured leader, for the way in which he has guided the war effort so far. I do not intend to recite the innumerable measures which have been taken by him and the members of his cabinet, but we can judge their wisdom by the results thus far, results which have called for unstinted praise from that grand man, Winston Churchill, and many leading men of the empire, as well as of the great republic to the south of us.
I want to thank my leader for the stand he has taken with respect to the future war effort. I must admit that for several weeks prior to my coming here I was somewhat disturbed as to the action the government might take, in view of the vociferous call for conscription for overseas service in the army, which has come from various sections of the dominion, but more particularly centred in certain interests in Toronto and Montreal. While I realize that the greatest energy is emanating from those interests who are trying to get rid of my leader and get control of the purse-strings of the government, I also realize there are a large number of loyal citizens who conscientiously believe that to carry on our maximum war effort we must put into effect conscription of men for the fighting forces. There are, on the other hand, many people who are opposed to this idea and are not of the opinion that this is necessary at the present time, some who feel that total war effort does not require the forcible calling up of men and placing them in combatant units and sending them overseas. I believe, too, that these people are just as loyal as any Canadians and 'are conscientious in their beliefs. On both sides of the controversy we have extremists, and I was worried as to what action the government might take. I was greatly relieved when I listened to the speech from the throne and found that members of parliament supporting the government were not going to be forced to break their promises to their constituents, if they wished to support the government and maintain a stable administration in control.
I am supporting the plebiscite. I want the government of the day to be relieved of their past commitments. I want the people of my constituency to tell this government, by their

'ote, to go ahead and do what they think advisable at any time, when in the light of their knowledge and judgment they decide upon a course they deem necessary in the best interests of the whole of Canada and the empire. I have faith in the loyalty and the judgment of the Canadians in my constituency of Westmorland and in all the other constituencies in the other provinces of Canada. I do not want to face the people of my constituency and have them say I am supporting a government that so flagrantly will ignore pledges. I have faith in Canada; I have faith in our people; I have faith in the love and loyalty of the mothers and fathers, even though some speakers who have preceded me may not. I am certain that true Canadians will sacrifice themselves, their sons and their daughters, if and when they believe those sacrifices are necessary to preserve our country and maintain our freedom and liberty for future Canadians. Personally, I do not believe in conscripting men for fighting units unless it is absolutely impossible to get men by any other means. During the last war we raised and maintained, as an effective fighting force in France, four grand infantry divisions, each one of which was classed as a first-line division and could be relied upon as first-line storm troops. Lloyd George once said:
The Canadians played a part of such distinction in the Somme battle of 1916 that thenceforward they were marked out as storm troops.
Was that because Canadians are superior beings to those of the motherland? Was it not because these divisions were made up of men who went over there voluntarily and were kept to their purpose by their own eagerness to do their part in destroying those forces that would destroy us? They did not go because they were forced; they went because they elected to do so of their own free will. The troops we have sent across the sea during this war are made up of just that kind of men, and there are many yet ready to go to support them. Do hon. members think it advisable to reinforce those troops from the ranks formed by men pressed into service against their will. I do not wish to belittle those who will not volunteer to fight overseas, but I do not consider that it is to the best interests of the Canadian army to dilute it with men so constituted that they have not the heart and spirit to fight, and who must be driven on by compulsion. Let the farmers go on the land, the machinists work in the shops, and by all means send only those into the combatant units who have the intestinal fortitude to go.
In spite of the flagrant statements made in this house, and outside this house, I do not

The Address-Mr. Emmerson
believe that our voluntary system has fallen down. I am still of the opinion that we can raise, by voluntary means, all the troops we should. From the beginning of this war till the end of 1941 our voluntary enlistments for all branches of the service have been over
422,000,	and apparently it is keeping up, for over 182,000 were attested during the calendar year of 1941. The first month of this year, January, has given us, by voluntary enlistment for overseas, over 11,000 men for the army alone, and I am confident that there will be a continuous flow answering Canada's call. These men, together with the "R" recruits that are being called up under the National War Services Act, will tax the resources of our training facilities, and it will keep this country on its toes to supply and equip them, in the light of the tremendous demands for all the guns, tanks, rifles, et cetera, that are so urgently needed by the empire and our allies w'here they are actually struggling with our vicious enemies.
The government has announced in parliament that the Canadian corps overseas is to be expanded to an army of two corps; one to be a corps of three infantry divisions and two army tank brigades; the other to consist of two armoured divisions. The navy is to take all the ships Canada can produce, and man them just as soon as they can be put into commission. There is to be an increase in the home war establishment of the air force as well. With that extension of the army, there are all the corps and army -ancillary troops, which, with the reserves to be sent forward this year, will require around 95,000 men- to be enlisted, trained, and equipped up to March, 1943. There is every reason to believe that this can and will be done by voluntary enlistment.
I think Canadians are prepared and eager to enlist, equip and maintain as large a fighting force as we are physically able to do. But there is a limit bey-ond which Canada cannot go and make our forces effective. Do not let us forget that at the present time we have about 550,000 men and 75,000 women working in our factories on war production, and remember also that during the last war there were less than half that number of men engaged in war production. Let us also keep in mind the very large number of men in the air force, at least 100,000 enlisted men, besides the civilian personnel in the empire training scheme, and upwards of 27,000 in the Royal Canadian Navy, which has done such heroic work in guarding our shores and convoying the ships carrying food and munitions to Great Britain and our allies, who are so much in need of them. All these tremendous efforts
of our country require men, but they require machines even more, in this type of war. Those of us who made u-p the Canadian corps of 1914-18 have still vivid memories of the trenches and the holes in the ground to and through which we foot-slogged it, but our army of to-day -moves on wheels or treads, with engines, transmissions, and drives, that need specially trained -men to operate and maintain them. I do not think I am very far out of the way in saying that the striking power of one of our divisions to-day is equal to that of two of the divisions of the last great war, and that the modem division requires far more men behind the lines and at home -to equip and maintain it in the field.
Mr. Speaker, I have faith in our government, and- I have every reason to have that faith when I know' the type of men who make up our government. We are fortunate, especially at this time, in having such men, so many of whom know by experience as soldiers what it is to fight a war, and know what it is to hear the thud of a shell and the whine of a bullet too unpleasantly near. No one can doubt their loyalty, and no one should question their determination to make a full and total war effort. I shall support the government in this plebiscite, and I shall support this government should circumstances so develop that they feel it necessary to enact total conscription for the army for action in any part of the world where it is necessary to fight the enemy.
The other night I had the privilege of listening to a lecture in the theatre of the National Museum in Ottawa on the subject of "Canada's Army-Man-Power Plus Machines". The speaker was Lieutenant-Colonel Goforth of the headquarters staff, Department of National Defence. I have confidence in our military leaders and our military staff, even thohgh one of the speakers the other evening said a great deal that might cause the people of this country to doubt their ability. Among other things, Colonel Goforth told his audience that a comprehensive study had been made by our military authorities some time prior to the present W'ar, and it was concluded that the maximum force that could be raised in Canada and maintained in action was six infantry divisions and one cavalry division. At that time, so far as one could gather from the speaker, there was no idea of any British empire air training scheme, nor could there have been at that time any comprehension of the huge proportions to which the production of arms add implements of war in Canada would be expanded, not to mention the growth and expansion of the Royal Canadian Navy.

The Address-Mr. Emmerson

Have we not already accomplished more than it was ever hoped we could? Can there be any justice in claiming that this government has not gone all-out under the inspiration of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King)? Could there be anything more unfair than the accusation or the insinuation that William Lyon Mackenzie King has had any other idea than an all-out war effort? One thing certain is that a maximum war effort can be accomplished only by making it a united effort. Up to the present time no one can say that there has not been evidence of a unity of purpose in this country such as has never before prevailed' in Canada. What a sabotaging of the war effort it would be if those who are so eager to upset the government or destroy its leader should for this or any other reason succeed in setting one section of Canada against the other. '
There is actually just one point on which the opposition differs from the government, and that is as to the method of securing men for the army overseas. Surely there is only one way to decide what Canada wants. Let us ask the people whose servant we are. Let me ask those who oppose the plebiscite, are we to be hypocrites preaching democracy and practising totalitarianism? We must not be stampeded into Hitler's methods by catch-phrases and extreme statements. Let us get down to calm thinking. The cost of the plebiscite in dollars will not be too high a price to pay for our democratic ideals of government. When we know that our implements of war and equipment are being given to those who so urgently need them right now in battle, and that men are being trained by Canada as rapidly as our facilities will permit, what delay will there be in our war effort by holding a plebiscite? What right have you or I on either side of this house to say that the people should not be given a chance to speak their mind in the only way in which they can effectively do so, and why should opposition members on the other side fear the sound of that voice? Who are we to feel that the people of Canada are not every bit as loyal to Canada as members of this chamber and as eager to go the limit in defeating the enemy at every point we can?
Our duty is clear. Winston Churchill has made it clear to us. He said:
Bach to our part, each to our station. Bill the armies, rule the air, pour out the munitions, strangle the U-boats, sweep the mines, plough the land, build the ships, guard the streets, succour the wounded, uplift the downcast and honour the brave.
Let us go forward together in all parts of the empire, in all parts of this island. There is not a week, not a day, nor an hour to be lost.

Do not let us becloud the issue; and if each gets busy and makes it clear to our constituents, I am sure Canadians will tell the world they absolve the government of the day from any commitment that might interfere in a full, all-out conduct of the war effort.
Mr. J. E. S. EMMANUEL D'ANJOU (Rimouski) (Translation): Mr. Speaker, realizing my responsibility as a member for the constituency of Rimouski, at this time, and with all possible frankness, I wish to state my opinion concerning the plebiscite mentioned in the speech from the throne. Having always been a Liberal, I have, for the last thirty years, campaigned for my party, not only in my own constituency, but in a large part of the provinces of Quebec, Ontario and New Brunswick. Follower of Laurier and Lapointe and, I may add, follower of the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), I have always believed in their political creed for, to me, the word Liberal has always meant freedom of thought and speech on all political matters.
Therefore, on the strength of this very freedom, I shall, in all frankness and without reservation, state my reasons for opposing the plebiscite alluded to in the speech from the throne. In my estimation, the proposed plebiscite may have but one outcome, that is conscription for overseas service purely and simply. It is nothing but a screen through which the hideous outline of conscription is plainly visible. I have always been opposed to	conscription	for	service
outside of Canada and to-day, more than ever, I am against this iniquitous system of military enlistment.
Furthermore, no power on earth could cause me to repudiate the solemn pledges that I gave to my faithful constituents on this matter of conscription. I have stated time and again in each parish of my constituency, that I should	oppose	whoever in	this	houseattempted to enforce compulsory military service for overseas. I even specified that I would not hesitate to vote against my party if it ever took that initiative. I shall therefore keep	my word and vote	against theaddress and the plebiscite. I repeat that, to my mind, the plebiscite is the forerunner of conscription, for the government, unless they intend to	enact a	measure of	this	nature,
would not ask to be relieved of past commitments in this connection. The risk is too great and the most elementary discretion commands that I remain on the alert and watch my step.
However, I must say that I rely entirely on the right hon. Prime Minister. But how am I

The Address-Mr. D'Anjou
to know how long he will remain at the head of the government. He does not enjoy immortality any more than we do. And death may come suddenly. We have experienced the truth of this statement, some time ago, on the occasion of the decease of the late Minister of Justice, Mr. Lapointe.
It is, however, my honest hope, for the greatest good of the country, that the right hon. Prime Minister may long remain at the head of the government. But, I repeat that, for any one of many reasons, he may disappear from the political arena, and I am not prepared, in advance, to trust his successor in the matter of conscription for overseas service.
Our political opponents, Mr. Speaker, have often stated that the province of Quebec stood alone in its opposition to conscription. The verdict rendered on March 26, 1940, however, has shown this statement to be false. Both political parties made known their opposition to conscription and the present government was returned to power by the greatest majority ever obtained at any previous general election in Canada. It can be proven, if need be, that Frencli-Canadians from the province of Quebec and from Rimouski constituency in particular are neither poltroons nor cowards. During the last war, a regiment from Rimouski went overseas and counted among its brave men, Jean Brillant and Joseph Iieable. Both received the highest military honour within the gift of Great Britain, the Victoria Cross. A constituency boasting such heroes does not deserve to see its population be referred to as people who refuse to fight and flinch in the accomplishment of duty.
In company with several of my colleagues who have spoken before me, I stand wholeheartedly for the defence of Canada, but of Canada only and on Canadian soil. Since Japan came into the war, our country is in greater danger than ever before. Why not keep our men here, then, in case the country should be attacked? Australia has had her own sorrowful, experience. Australia sent many of her best troops to foreign lands. She is calling for help to-day, because she is insufficiently defended and lacks the number of men required to cope with the situation.
In so far as I am concerned, Mr. Speaker, may I say that when the time comes to answer the plebiscite my answer will be no, and I will advise my electors to give the same reply.
I do not wish the government to be released from, their undertaking nor do I wish to be released myself. The members of the government were not alone in their pledge against conscription. All hon. members of this house
gave the same undertaking. I intend to vote against the subamendment, against the amendment itself and against the main motion.
I do believe, Mr. Speaker, it would be political wisdom on the part of the government were they to change the. Mobilization Act so as to exempt farmers' sons and farm hands from its application. I have had occasion quite often in my constituency, which is essentially agricultural, to ask for postponements on behalf of farmers' sons. I might quote, among other instances, two really sad cases. An excellent old man, a farmer, seventy-six years of age and sick, had three sons. Two of them were already undergoing training and he came to me in the hope that I might obtain a postponement for the remaining son. Would you believe it, Mr. Speaker, I was unable to obtain this, and notwithstanding the fact that his other two sons were already in training they took the last one from him. Such a course does not seem reasonable, for wars are not won by soldiers alone, especially by soldiers who have nothing to eat. Soldiers have to be fed if they are to fight. In order to provide them with food, the farms have to be operated.
Here is another case. A widow with a large farm, asked me to obtain a postponement for her only son. I have been unable to obtain it. The exemption boards should show more consideration, especially in the case of farmers' sons.
As I said a moment ago, Mr. Speaker, I am in favour of defending Canada and Canada alone, for I am first of all a Canadian. Mine is the motto of Sir Wilfrid Laurier: Canada first, Canada always, Canada only. May I quote the following words uttered by Lord Tweedsmuir, a former governor general of Canada:
Canada is a sovereign nation and cannot take her attitude docilely from Britain, or from the United States, or from anybody else. A Canadian's first loyalty is not to the British Commonwealth of Nations, but to Canada and Canada's king, and those who deny this are doing, to my mind, a great disservice to the commonwealth.
I conclude, Mr. Speaker, by stating once again my intention to vote against the address in reply to the speech from the throne, that is, against the plebiscite mentioned therein.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to add my voice to those who are asking for a better deal for the farmer. We are hoping that the government will see fit to recognize the extreme value of an organized farm effort in relation to our war effort. The farmer has been hit harder by the war than those in any other vocation.
The Address-Mr. Aylesworth

He has been hit from all sides-by the shortage of farm labour, by the low prices of his products, by the high prices of his necessities and now by the price ceiling, which was applied before the prices of his products reached parity with the prices of the goods he must buy. In the old days the farmer, when he had to give his best days to working on the soil, retired to the city or town and left the farm to the young people. They did the hard work after that. Now the young people leave the farm long before the old people are ready to retire. In the city the young people can make a living without much effort, and there is no inducement to them to return to the farm where they can barely make a living, and that only with a good deal of effort. As a result, the old people are left to struggle along, and when they can no longer carry the burden alone they must- hire help.
With the beginning of the war the demand from industry for all kinds of workers at good wages resulted in hired men being weaned away from the farm to industry. Unless the farmer can compete with industry in the matter of wages-and very few of them can-a very serious situation will have to be faced. We should have a war plan for the farmer. No one can rise in his place in this house and say that the farmer has been receiving fair prices for his products in the past; that is, prices that are fair in relation to the prices the farmer has to pay for the commodities he has to buy.
Unfortunately, most city people do not know the farmer. They think that all he has to do is to plant seeds, wait for the product to grow and then harvest it and sell it. They do not realize the backaching work that goes into his job, the heartaches from wind, hail, drought and floods/ to say nothing of insect pests. Certainly he has had his good years, but even in those times his profits have not been large, and in the bad years his optimism has kept him going. On the whole the farmer has done little complaining to the government about his plight. Perhaps if he had done more complaining, he would not be in the position he is in to-day. The prices he receives at present barely assure him his existence, and there is no relief in sight.
This ties up with the labour problem. If the food production industry gets a parity of prices, it will be able to pay wages comparable with those paid by industry. With the rise in price of most farm products owing to the war, it looked as if the farmer might soon have an adequate return for his efforts and be put in a position where he would be able to compete with industry for help. But then came the

price ceiling. The farmer does not object to the government's action in this regard provided a fair balance of prices is maintained. There is injustice to the farmer in freezing the unbalanced economy that exists, and I suggest to the government that the price ceiling should be let off certain products. The farmer should have a fair return for the products he sells.
So little consideration is being given the farmer that it looks as if the government does not realize the importance of keeping the farmer in production, and more production. Canada has been struggling along with a hand-to-mouth policy, and it is evident that if the country is to hold its own in the task of sending food to war-torn Britain and feed its own population, including the army, the navy and air force, some plan must be advised to -bring farms into full production.
Some people say, "What if we bring the farms into full production and the war ends?" That would be good. Just think of the enormous market there would be in starving Europe, for food, as well as the huge market that would exist to replenish the herds of live stock in European countries. We have been in this war considerably longer than the United States, and already they have a plan for agriculture, while our plan, if we have any, is piecemeal and has no definite goal. If we do not plan now for agricultural production, there is grave danger of a food shortage in the country.
At the last session of parliament the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) put forward a plan for agricultural production, and a very good plan it was. In fact, it might bear repeating. But has the government taken any note of it? Let me repeat some of his suggestions. First of all, there is the suggestion to appoint a national food board. I know that the wartime prices and trade board and the agricultural supply board are operating, but they are not planning to any extent for future production. They are interested in controlling prevailing production. This board would estimate the production required for 1942, and each year to the end of the war, to feed Canada and meet the requirements of our allies. Canada would be divided into production zones according to the things best produced in the different areas. Give this board power to put into operation any scheme whereby the maximum production for the zone would be reached, and assure adequate supplies of labour, with machinery and fertilizers made available for agricultural purposes. There should be nothing difficult about this.
National registration has shown that there are sufficient men to work the farms if they

The Address-Mr. Aylesworth
are placed at this work. We could even recruit a farm army at military pay and place them in the different zones as needed. As for machinery, the government could arrange transportation to any point where needed, or make it part of the equipment of the farm army.
Another suggestion was a women's farm army. The Ontario government is going to and may now be training women to take their places on the farm. Could not the federal government follow their lead and recruit women for farm work? I would earnestly urge upon the government that farmers' sons and farm help working on the farms and producing food be allowed to continue this work.
With regard to parity for farm prices with war production, I mentioned before when I suggested withholding the price ceiling to allow farm products to catch up and gain parity.	.
The board would provide that the owner of the land would have these objectives and would be adequately reimbursed for his investment and his effort. That is only fair, because all other industries receive a fair return. Give the farmers fair markets and sufficient help and they will keep our farms producing. The board would plan to build up stocks of finished foods like canned pork and beef, canned vegetables, evaporated milk, dried eggs, and so on. I would make only one addition to the plan of the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe, that is that a special section of the national food board deal with and promote a greatly increased production of cattle and hogs. The demand for bacon from our allies is ever increasing. Someone slipped so badly in their estimate of the requirements of our allies that for a time we were asked not to buy pork, with the result that the price of other meats climbed so high it was cheaper to buy pork. I admit that the situation in this regard has improved, but we could have an even greater production in hogs. For instance, we have a huge surplus of wheat that could be purchased from the western farmer at a fair price and sold to the hog raisers of Ontario. The government could arrange this. With the feed problem solved, the farmer could raise twice as many hogs. We should also increase the number of cattle raised, not only for food but in order to be ready at the end of the war to send many shiploads to Europe for food and for stock.
Cattle demand for the past year has been 115,247 head greater than for 1940. The main reasons for this increase were: curtailment of supplies of pork for home consumption; increased industrial activity resulting in improved consumer purchasing power; and the
fact that military camp estimated requirements were 40,211,767 pounds, compared with 18,214,421 pounds in 1940, an increase of 21,997,346 pounds. At an average of 500 pounds to the carcase the increase is equal to 44,000 head of cattle. This makes a total camp consumption of 80,000 cattle. The number of cattle on feed is below that for the past five years. Incidentally I am sure our producers are looking for higher prices, to offset the higher prices paid for feeding cattle, the increased cost of feed and higher wages of farm help.
An improved demand for beef in both Canada and the United States could easily bring about a period when marketings of cattle would fall short of supplying our full requirements of beef. It is important that our producers be encouraged to increase their production, so I ask that the ceiling price on beef be lifted for a time. I ask the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) to see that producers of beef, lamb and hogs are allowed to make a reasonable profit.
I would also ask the government to allow the price of cheese to advance. The lifting of the ceiling, allowing the price of cheese made during the winter to advance, was a good thing, but many farmers were not able to produce milk during the winter months and, therefore, could not take advantage of this.
I should like to place before the house the necessity of encouraging an increase in lamb production. We are facing a shortage of wool in this country, and that at a time when woollen mills are coming to Canada from England. Also last year we imported nearly
3,000,000 pounds of lamb. I should like to place on record these figures showing our imports of lamb from Australia and New Zealand from 1934 to 1941:

There was a very healthy demand for lamb in 1941. This demand was doubtless due to increased purchasing power of consumers, and also to curtailment in pork supplies. The above figures show the effect of the reduction in import duties. The ceiling price on lamb has recently been lifted. This is in accord with my view, and I would ask
The Address-Mr. Aylesworth

that it be left off in order to encourage production. If we could produce the 3,000,000 pounds of lamb imported last year, it would equal 70,000 lambs, which would produce 500 000 pounds of wool.
The farmers also have to face the restriction of electric power, and I would ask the government to give every consideration through their power controller to applications for electric power in order to help in the production of the necessary foodstuffs.
This country, Mr. Speaker, is facing a grave situation. What happened in France should be a lesson to us. Party politics and shades of political opinion so divided that country and created such dissension that it was impossible to obtain any cooperation or continuity of effort toward the prosecution of a war. At this time when we are facing such an emergency party politics should be forgotten. Anything said at this time should be aimed toward unity rather than tending to create dissension among the Canadian people. What has happened to Australia may happen any day to Canada, and it is important that we do the right thing now. I appreciate the effort the government has already put forth but I would earnestly urge a still greater effort. Russia is calling for more equipment; China is calling for more equipment; General McNaughton asks for more and better equipment; so let us see that every man or woman who can work is put to work, and let us produce to the very limit of our resources. Surely it is time we became alive to the fact that we stand in a very precarious position, from which we can extricate ourselves only by a determined effort on the part of all the people.

speechtext:
With very much of what the hon. member for Frontenac-Addington (Mr. Aylesworth) has just said I am in hearty agreement. Probably that is no wonder, because we both represent constituencies very much interested in the agricultural life of this country. I congratulate the hon. member upon what he has said.
This debate is now in its third week. Such being the situation I shall not cover all the ground I had intended to, because much of what I expected to say has been well expressed by other hon. members.
The hun is at our gates; the Jap is at our gates, our gates both east and west; Canada's gates both east and west. If there ever was a time in the history of our country when clear thinking without political or personal bias was required from members of parliament, this is the time. Having regard to this, I was sorry to see so many members of the opposition resort to making political speeches for seven-

eighths of their time and then in the remaining one-eighth trying to fool the house and the country by striking a patriotic note.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: What about the hon. member for Parry Sound (Mr. Slaght) this afternoon?

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman made
his speech, so please let me make mine. Surely it has been demonstrated again that the Tory party, shorn of power, is like a she bear robbed of her cubs. I am free to admit that certain members of the Liberal party have dealt somewhat with politics in part of their remarks, but I am sure that an unbiased perusal of the record will show that such statements were provoked by opposition speeches. Occupying as I do one of the buffer seats in this parliament, as I also did in the last parliament, with opposition members to the left and opposition members to the front, I can truthfully say that for the most part I have found them splendid fellows. I believe many of them are gradually coming to the Liberal viewpoint. I urge them to continue to seek the light, because I feel that without leaders they will have to wind up as a party. During the few years I have been in parliament I have endeavoured to follow the motto: "If you have nothing to say, say nothing." May I suggest to those groups sitting to the far left that if democracy is to function as intended, they should pay more attention to this motto. I have on my desk the following verse:
What one approves, another scorns,
And thus each his nature shows.
You find the rose bush full of thorns;
I find the thorn bush full of roses.
I often turn to this for comfort when I hear or read of some move that does not appeal to me.
The hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Black) is a friend of long standing, whom I admire in both a business and personal way. I cannot, however, follow his political thought. On Monday, while speaking of the accomplishments of his constituency in munition manufacturing, it seemed to me that he was not at ease, that he cast his eyes down, and I hope he bowed his head. He must have recalled that but two short years ago he was touring his county far and wide and in effect saying that the statement made by the late Norman Rogers, a fellow-townsman, on behalf of the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe), that a large aeroplane programme was under way for Amherst was nothing but election talk, and that if Amherst was to have a revival of industry it would be necessary to elect the Manion National government. The Manion government was not elected, and the

The Address-Mr. Purdy
hon. gentleman sits condemned by his own words and discredited in the eyes of many of his electors by the statements he made at that time.
The constituency I have the honour to represent, Colehester-Hants, has its roots far back in the days of colonization in Nova Scotia, and stretches from Northumberland strait to the bay of Fundy, across the central part of the province. Truro, the shire town of Colchester, was the Cobequid of the Acadian;, and Windsor, the shire town of Hants county, the Pisquid. Our people are mostly of British origin, the forefathers of many of them being New England planters or pre-loyalists, who took up the lands from which the Acadians were expelled prior to the American revolution. They were followed by their Loyalist friends and relatives, and the ties with the British isles were strengthened by direct emigration from England, Scotland and Ireland. We have a small percentage of other European stock, and a considerable overflow from the original German or Dutch settlements in Lunenburg county. Our population is roughly one-third urban and two-thirds rural. The chief industries of the towns are textiles, lumber products, wood pulp, dairy products and fertilizers. The principal activities in the country are mixed farming and lumbering. Large quantities of gypsum are produced round the famous Minas basin, where the tides rise as high as sixty feet; and the western end of the constituency is the eastern end of the famous Annapolis valley, so that we produce about one-tenth of the commercial apple crop of the province.
With this background and these surroundings, Mr. Speaker, we have maintained a reasonably well balanced economy and have produced a race of people loyal to the British crown and British traditions, proud to call the union jack our flag. When the call for duty came, our boys and girls were no less willing to enlist than in the past, and are now serving wherever Canadians are found on the far-flung battle front. They are standing firm on British shores, flying over the low countries and in the middle east, and their names appear on the service rolls with the Hong Kong heroes. One company of the forestry corps now serving overseas was largely recruited in our district. We are represented in the prison camps of Germany, and our casualty lists are mounting. Enlistments keep up. To those who do not return I pay my homage. While not regarded as a marine constituency compared with others in the province, our boys have enlisted freely in the Royal Canadian Navy, and their names can be found in large numbers among the unsung heroes of the war,
the merchant marine. One of my constituents, Mr. Dick Harvie, of Noel Road, Hants county, has seven sons serving with the forces, volunteers for service anywhere. That is a truly magnificent contribution from any one home.
Let me say here to these men and women of the forces, to many of whom I am tied by the bonds of friendship, and to others by the ties of blood, and to their relations and friends, that as their representative in the parliament of Canada I hope and pray they will feel that in the decisions we have made or are required to make I have not and will not let them down. I voted for the Union government in 1917 because I felt then, as I feel to-day, that selective service is the fair way of raising an army. But, Mr. Speaker, war as practised to-day by our enemies is not fair war, and we must meet them by the most efficient methods at which the best brains of this country can arrive.
In case I may be misunderstood I will say here and now that if it develops that the voluntary method of raising men does not produce sufficient recruits to maintain overseas the maximum force we are capable of sending, having regard to the demands on our man-power for munitions and supplies and adequate home defence, I will support the government in extending the provisions of the National Resources Mobilization Act to cover man-power for overseas. Churchill, in his famous speech to the empire after Dunkirk, called us to our stations-not necessarily in the firing line, but wherever we were most useful. Since munitions, food and ships are now required rather than man-power, Canada must, on account of her location, be expected to take a larger share of the load in this regard than otherwise would be the case. This is not nearly as spectacular as the million marching feet asked for by some of the opposition, but it is far more effective in an allout, balanced effort. It was German machines, not man-power, that drove through the low countries, raced up the French lines and drove the British expeditionary force into the sea at Dunkirk. We must equip our army and the armies of our allies with the very latest in fighting equipment before we lessen the flow of these vital articles overseas by drawing men from the production lines. Have we the man-power to keep up the maximum supply of munitions and food and at the same time materially increase our overseas force? I do not know. We look to the government to inform us and to lead us in an all-out war effort, with a complete mobilization of all resources, material and human. I urge that
The Address-Mr. Purdy

in such an effort our natural resources must be further developed and more advantage taken of the productive capacity of our smaller mncerns than has been the case to date.
As yet, Mr. Speaker, I fear that our manpower and productive capacity are a long way from being fully mobilized, and that a great deal of our effort is still devoted to nonessentials. The people of Canada are just now beginning to feel the pinch of regulations which are necessary for the carrying out of the war. This being the situation, they look to the government not only to regulate and advise, but also to set an example. It is therefore difficult to understand how certain departments can continue to use up manpower and materials along certain lines in duplication and non-essential services, while other departments are crying for the people to salvage and save, and our allies are looking to us to produce more munitions.
For instance, our Post Office Department has a considerable programme of expensive advertising. Their service should be their best advertiser. If they are advocating less use of the telegraph, one department of government is in effect working against another. Again, wTe have recently been favoured with a series of advertisements issued by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. These were very well done, but, I would assume, very expensive. Surely present radio listeners do not have to be told what the corporation is doing, and we are supposed to discourage the purchase of more radios. Could not the materials and man-power used in these activities be placed to better advantage elsewhere?
Again, we have one department of the government sending out forms all across the country, asking from business certain information which has already been furnished to another department, or continuing to send out the inquiries when the party to whom they are addressed has advised that he does not deal in the article or articles inquired about.
I have before me an inquiry which has been widely circulated, asking for the price of bread on certain recent dates, while the price has been pegged throughout Canada since the outbreak of war. Is this efficiency or economy? Is it any wonder that the maritime boards of trade, at a recent meeting, asked that business be released from the work of furnishing so many government returns?
In my constituency are located the Debert military camp, the Debert airport and the Stanley elementary training school. At these
I Mr. Purdy.]
various centres in the course of their training, or sailing for overseas, we are privileged to have a large number of the picked manhood of Canada, not only of Canada but of all parts of the British commonwealth, and also of the United States. Our citizens have welcomed these strangers with open arms, and while, having regard to the numbers of men as compared with our population, we have not been able to do all we would wish, yet I consider that most of our temporary military guests will take away with them very warm feelings toward the people of this banner constituency. Surely this contact will, in the years to come, bear fruit, and people from other provinces and other lands will be better able to understand our problems and we theirs.
In passing, it might be well to point out to the Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power) that from reliable sources I am informed that the Stanley school was the only one in eastern Canada able to carry on continual flying operations last spring during the break-up, and suggest that our location is most suitable for further extensions if required.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I feel I should refer to a matter which has to some extent caused me to lose my faith in mankind. I am told on good authority that in the officers' mess at Debert and at other military camps the story is being circulated that the reason why a large military camp was established at Debert is because the site of it was the old Ralston homestead and was owned by our present Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston). A return filed on February 9 to an order of this house of February 2 shows that the land occupied at this point was acquired from more than 120 individual owners and that none was owned by the hon. minister. In fact I can obtain no information that either he or his near relatives ever owned property in this district. The hon. minister, who in 1914 and again in 1939 answered the call of his country, is too big a man to pay attention to such lies as the one I have mentioned, apparently circulated in order to discredit the government, but I feel that this statement of the true situation should be posted in every mess of the Canadian army so that he who runs may read. Officers who are gentlemen should know how to deal with the likes of those who start stories such as the one to which I have referred.
Coming now to the plebiscite, I propose to support it, and urge my constituents to vote, "Yes". Why do I do this? I do this because I feel that our ministry should have a free hand, subject only to the control of parliament, in the troublesome days to come.

The Address-Mr. Purdy
Do I feel that the government is bound by a pledge of ''no conscription for overseas service" given in 1940? My answer is "yes". Furthermore, I consider, having accepted the Liberal platform and having been elected on same, that I am also bound by the pledge. It may be hard for our opponents to get over the idea that election promises are made to be elected on and then to be forgotten, but my leader, the Prime Minister, stands for something higher than that, and I feel that the people of Canada will honour him for the stand he has taken, in spite of the clamour of the old Tories for him to forget promises. Surely, had he done so, he would have to-day been held up to the Canadian people as a man whose promise could not be relied upon, and this by the same people who are now condemning him for holding the plebiscite.
Mr. Speaker, may I take a few moments to refer to my part of the country. I referred previously to a full use of the productive capacity of our smaller plants, of which we have a number capable of doing something to help along the war effort, but so far they have been given very little opportunity. In fact one has had to close entirely owing to the lack of raw materials, and others to curtail. When the Minister of Munitions and Supply announced the bits-and-pieces programme last fall, I felt that it was a splendid move, and I strongly urge that it be developed until every shop and every bit of machinery capable of producing a needed article for our war effort are at work. I have asked on many occasions that small concerns in my constituency as well as our contractors be given consideration on war and defence projects. To date, for the most part, we have had to be content with the crumbs which fall from the rich man's table. Centralization is efficient to a certain point but, if carried beyond that point, creates inefficiency.
I would suggest that the time is now ripe for the government to take industry to where the labour and facilities are available rather than make it necessaiy for the people from the maritimes to move to central Canada to work, with the consequential housing and transportation problems, to say nothing of post-war situations and the disarrangement of our local economy.
Our contractors are efficient and should have been given an equal chance on local defence works rather than being overlooked until the best contracts in the district were given to central Canadian firms, some without our contractors knowing that the project was open. Even on tenders advertised in the public press, maritime contracts are at
times advertised in the central Canada media, while I have yet to see central Canada projects of a similar nature advertised in our local papers.
Equal sacrifice should mean equal opportunity, and I would urge that we be given this oportunity. To my mind this can be brought about only by a better geographical distribution of the various appointments in key positions in the departments charged mainly with our -war effort.
In the past the maritime provinces have not been found lacking in producing men of a high calibre, nor are they to-day, and I believe that if the course I have suggested is followed, we shall have made a further step toward a balanced and all-out war effort.
Not so long ago the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services (Mr. Macdonald), our then premier, was called to Ottawa by the Prime Minister. Our people felt honoured by this action. I recall hearing the present Minister of National Defence for Naval Services say at one time that a happy and contented peasantry was the back-bone of a country.
As stated previously, approximately two-thirds of my constituency is rural, many of these being engaged in. mixed farming. May I, therefore, for a -moment be permitted to deal with some of their problems. It will be recalled that prior to the price-ceiling policy being announced, the position of our eastern farmers had been receiving attention and that it was decided t-hat, in the face of the low prices they were receiving for their products, some assistance was in order. The federal government agreed to pay one-third of the freight on feed grains, and the local government the same. Then we come to the priceceiling policy when, to bring farm products somewhere in line with other ceiling prices, the *western farmers were given further assistance and the eastern farmers the full freight on feed grain. As stated a moment ago, our farmers had previously been given, based on their need of assistance, two-thirds of the freight, so the assistance they in fact received was but one-third. It therefore seems to me that in order to carry out the intention of the priceceiling policy our farmers should receive additional assistance to the equivalent of two-thirds freight on western feed grains. This can be arranged by way of a rebate or discount on feed purchased, and I would ask the government to consider this matter.
Some of our farmers and poultrymen were surprised to find that western corn was not included for freight assistance, although it had been included in the original discussions. It

The Address-Mr. Purdy

was included in the British Columbia agreements. Apparently the Ontario corn growers had to be protected at the expense of the maritimes. The matter was taken up with the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), and hopes were held out for its inclusion by special arrangement. We are now advised after two months' delay that nothing can be done. I ask the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) to remove the duty on water-borne ;orn brought to the maritimes and suggest that ve now have reason to expect this. Our farmers are not organized, nor can they afford to send large delegations to Ottawa as their western cousins have recently done. If they had the money they would, under present conditions, buy war bonds or certificates and not spend it in taking long trips. If they took the trip, who would look after their work? Therefore, as a member from Nova Scotia, interested in the welfare of our farming population, as all our members are, I am speaking on their behalf.
I am not in accord with the system of bonuses built up for western agriculture and, if I understand the Prime Minister and the Minister of Agriculture correctly, about to be extended by new legislation; yet having regard to the price-ceiling policy, I see no other way of equalizing farm income with that of other industries.
If the end of the war is not to see the number of vacant farms in Nova Scotia largely increased, with resulting relief problems, something more must be done for agriculture.
I have shown what we are entitled to under the "some assistance" but not "equalization" price-ceiling policy. A series of abattoirs and cold storage warehouses might be erected in the province at places convenient to the mixed farming population, such as at Antigonish, Pictou, Truro, Windsor and Lunenburg. With such an arrangement our farmers could receive a proper inspection and price for their products locally, instead of shipping them out of the province or equally long distances to provincial points, only at times to have them returned for consumption within a few miles of where they were produced. I shall not further labour this matter, but suggest that it should be carefully considered.
In view of the labour situation on our farms brought about by enlistments, and higher wages being paid in war industries, assistance could be given in certain sections by way of extension of rural mail routes and assistance in extending rural electrification into districts not now eligible under provincial legislation. This latter would, of course, only be possible if the equipment were available.

Both these suggestions, if put into effect, would increase the number of man-hours available for work on the land.
Mr. Speaker, we have a wheat committee of the cabinet. I would suggest the appointment of an eastern agricultural committee also, and I call upon the Prime Minister and the ministers representing the maritime provinces, as well as the Minister of Agriculture, to take the maritime agricultural situation in hand before it is too late and submit any necessary legislation for the maritimes along with that proposed for the assistance of western agriculture. Only in this way can we have a happy and contented peasantry stretching across Canada and our rural population united in this our hour of greatest need.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,, it is a great honour' and a heavy responsibility to rise amidst the elected representatives of the nation to speak on behalf of one of the constituencies of my province, the constituency where I was born and brought up, whose people, kindly witnesses of my first experiences in business life, have given me signal evidence of their confidence in choosing me to present their thoughts, their feelings and their aspirations to parliament and to the government.
Verdun and Lasalle, the two highly cosmopolitan municipalities making up my electoral division, are, with their citizens of various extractions and traditions, languages and religions, veritable miniatures of Canada. Faced by the same problems of life and inspired by a common ideal, my fellow-citizens have built up two great cities which have impressed all the people of Canada and have more than once been cited as examples to all communities seeking progress in union, understanding and tolerance.
The city of Verdun, by far the more populous of the two, proudly stands third in my province and twelfth in all Canada. Among the responsibilities which this honour has imposed upon it, there is one which it has discharged in a particularly glorious fashion. I refer to the part it played in this country's effort during the last war. The Prince of Wales himself, during his trip to Canada in 1919, stated that Verdun was the city of the British empire which had, in proportion to population, placed the largest number of men under arms.
Twenty-five years have passed, and these years may have effected a considerable change in the proportions and the appearance of the constituency which I represent. However, the sense of solidarity and of unity in the presence of great causes, the love of country and of liberty, have in no way diminished, and

The Address-Mr. Cote
it is with rightful pride that I -can say in this house that Verdun has accepted wholeheartedly and generously its large share of the burden of the present war. Thus it is that every war service, every patriotic organization, of whatever nature, is represented in the constituency of Verdun and receives all the cooperation and the results expected. In addition, according to the statistics available, Verdun is once again in the very first rank of the Dominion's municipalities as regards the proportion of its sons in our three fighting services.
In this community, so highly representative of the various ethnical elements of our country, I have imperceptibly gathered, a fairly accurate conception of the patriotic sense of Canada. I find myself to-day in the presence of my fellow-members of this house, all charged, though in different degrees, with the leadership of our beloved country in this [DOT]most critical period of her history-.
Allied of her own free will with the great democracies, Canada has constituted herself the champion of the liberties of our Christian civilization and has bravely opposed the conquering march of the armies of German . paganism.
