The conflict which began by the devastation and enslaving of far-away countries has drawn closer to our shores, and our national life is now seriously threatened.
During the two years and a half which this world-wide conflict has lasted, Canada has not betrayed the cause she undertook to champion. Quite the contrary. With the ardour and patriotism which distinguishes her sons and the incalculable richness of her resources, this Dominion has, for the defence of her territory and of civilization, contributed to the heroes of the democracies which have retained their freedom a magnificent effort which has excited the admiration, nay the astonishment, of the civilized world.
I am a Canadian by birth and by inclination. Never before, however, have I felt such love, such pride for my country as when I had an opportunity to appreciate, at the beginning of the present session, the progress made in the last two and a half years and to visualize what our young nation has accomplished for the defence of our most sacred liberties, for the safeguard of our Christian civilization. And the sentiment thus entertained toward my country was equalled only by my admiration for him who, on that date of January 26, rendered an account of the manner in which his administration has carried on the war, and by my pride in sharing the political convictions of the greatest of Canadian statesmen and the most Canadian of our great statesmen.
The Right Hon. Mackenzie King, our Prime Minister, has made a clear, comprehensive and eloquent statement on a well balanced and most efficient war effort. It would be presumption on my part, therefore, being only a novice in public affairs, to attempt under such circumstances to describe our contribution in the present conflict. I would rather leave the people under the charm of that enlightening speech which old parliamentarians claim to have been one of the best ever made in the house by the Right Hon. Prime Minister.
May I be permitted, nevertheless, to bring out into bolder relief how that outstanding speech offers a fundamental explanation for the success of the gigantic task undertaken and a guarantee of its successful and really efficient accomplishment. Addressing myself in all sincerity to my fellow countrymen of every province and of every class of society, to all those who in these hours of trial pride themselves on being Canadians, I would state that we would never have accomplished one-half of what the country has contributed in two years to the successful prosecution of the war had we not had, as a foundation for our economic and military activities, both peace and unity in the land and the possibility of utilizing fully the energies which inevitably develop under such favourable conditions.
Had we been a divided country, in the throes of internal strife, far from withstanding the burden of a military effort -which one might be tempted to call out of proportion with our development and population, our country might well have become but another instrument of those infernal machinations so ably devised under Hitlerian diplomacy.
Quite the contrary, in the security of internal peace, Canada has achieved a splendid contribution, particularly during the year about to close.
Our country has been able to produce all the food required for domestic consumption and to meet the needs of an ally having a population five times our own number.
We have succesfully developed our armament production and are in a position to-day to arm and equip by our own means a modern division in a relatively short time.
We have built a navy capable of serving as escort and of protecting convoys going overseas and of giving chase to enemy submarines over the seven seas.
An all-Canadian and powerful air force patrols our coasts, guards over our convoys and patrols enemy skies in search of new targets.
Compulsory military training prepares our young men for the defence of our country on
The Address-Mr. Cote

Canadian soil, while voluntary recruiting enlists all who are willing to carry the fight [DOT],o the enemy wherever he may be encountered.
In short, the economic and military policy of the country has been managed with such wisdom, that the government would hear nothing but a chorus of praise and gratitude, if it were not for the uproar fostered through a certain section of the press by a handful of heirs to the Union cabinet of 1917 and to the disturbances bred by that administration.
Faced with facts, these agitators are forced to admit, occasionally, the efficiency of our war effort, in all fields. Some of the newspapers, the Ottawa Journal and the Financial Post, among others, engaged in that contemptible campaign of disparagement against the government, but in reality against our Prime Minister, have published wThole supplements admitting the efficiency of our country's contribution to the allied cause. I shall mention only their issues of January 30th and 31st respectively, where 32- and 15-page supplements are devoted to a review of the accomplishments of our industries and armed forces.
However, it seems that these people are not satisfied with the complete harmony that obtains all through our war effort. They must always recall the causes of the 1917 misunderstanding and, to this end, they have revived the old battle cry: "Canada cannot realize a total war effort without conscription of its youth for military service overseas."
The Prime Minister has answered their clamour with faultless logic supported by the most irrefutable statistics.
I need not quote again the figures that have already been given in this house to show how successful the voluntary system has been. Yet, notwithstanding the fact that in the seven last months voluntary enlistment in the three services of our armed forces has given an average monthly yield of over 20,000 men, whereas in the month that has just ended, 11,000 recruits were obtained for the army only, the same clamour is being raised about the so-called failure of the voluntary system and the necessity of immediate conscription for overseas service.
Fortunately, such is not the view of right-minded and sincere people, nor I think of the great majority of Canadian citizens. The constituency which I have the honour to represent, and where there are people of various races and creeds, strongly supports maintenance of the voluntary system of enlistment for overseas military service. So far as I am concerned, I am all the more willing to express the view's of my constituents on that subject as I am and will remain a supporter of the anticonscriptionist doctrine.

I shall not repeat the arguments advanced by my colleagues in this house whose views on that matter are similar to mine. I shall only add that conscription has been an utter failure during the last war, that from October, 1917, to November, 1918, a period of thirteen months, it yielded 83,355 men 22,000 of whom were granted temporary postponement for agricultural or other purposes. Consequently, during the above mentioned period, that system only yielded a monthly average of 4,720 men, most of whom could be called soldiers only because they wore a uniform and were subject to military discipline, as compared with the average number of 8,000 men who have enlisted every month since September last, and all of whom are proud soldiers conscious of the part they have to play in the army and determined to uphold the honour of their country. There are over
250,000	such volunteers in our active army, besides over 125,000 men in the air force and over 25,000 in the navy, making up, as at the 1st of January last, a total of well over 400,000 men who have voluntarily enlisted in our armed forces for service anywhere in the world. In order to appreciate better the importance of those figures, we must remember that our munitions and arms factories are now employing over 500,000 men and over 70,000 women, or tv'ice the number of workers that v'ere required by the same class of munitions factories during the last war. Yet. our country has only 11,500.000 inhabitants.
I am against conscription because I am in the first place opposed to any cause of disunion and misunderstanding in this country. Besides, I believe that it will not be necessary in so far as the constituency which I represent is concerned. The voluntary system has hitherto been highly successful and the same success can be maintained through the sincere and enlightened cooperation of all those who are called upon to exert some influence over their fellow citizens and public opinion in general.
Let the newspapers who have hitherto furthered the cause of disunion in this country stop their purely political and personal controversies and launch a campaign for voluntary enlistment, or at the very least, occasionally publish earnest appeals to young Canadians, a thing which they have hitherto carefully refrained from doing.
Let certain military men, probably well intentioned but ill advised, abandon the coercive means they have brought to bear upon the young men under compulsory military

The Address-Mr. Cote
training, for the questionable purpose of hastening their enlistment in the active army; the signing up of a recruit through such means has not the character of a free decision and more often as not it hurts the cause, in discouraging a relative or a friend of the recruit, who otherwise would probably be earnestly willing to enlist.
Let the government consider whatever measures may be necessary to give better treatment to privates and non-commissioned officers in the active army, or to increase their dependents' allowances, keeping in mind that the pecuniary remuneration offered to them must meet the competition of the salaries that are attracting them to munitions factories.
Thus, the deficiencies and imperfections of our voluntary system having been remedied, enlistments will reach a higher level and bring into our active army as many if not more young men than during the last months, when conditions were not always quite favourable. At that rate, it would be possible, within a year, to obtain at least 100,000 additional men, without prejudice to the needs of the air force or the navy. I have every reason to believe that conscription for service in the active army would not produce as good results in the same period, and I need not emphasize the dare consequences it would undoubtedly have upon the morale of our people.
Unity within our ranks is a prime condition of success for our arms. By uniting our hearts, our minds and our energies we will succeed, under the guidance of an enlightened and wise government, in putting to really good use all our material resources and man-power, in a way that will ensure victory for the democracies over the forces of evil. Without such unity, whatever those in authority may do, we cannot expect anything but halfmeasures and quite unsatisfactory results.
Mr. Speaker, let us make the most of what is likely to unite us in this war; let us make use of it fully in the best interests of the great cause which we must defend until victory. As to what is liable to divide the country and, mind you, it is only a very small part of our total war effort, let us examine it calmly, without prejudice or passion. Let us see if, by adopting a one-sided and inflexible solution, we are not jeopardizing the ever growing successes which have crowned our efforts in this domain as well as in all the others.
The Prime Minister and his government have succeeded in preserving peace and harmony in our country since the beginning of the war. Unity has been preserved in the country by a responsible and strong government, in which the nation had placed full confidence. Conditions have arisen which have been considered to necessitate an appeal to the people on the question of compulsory military service. I need not question the motives which governed this decision. I have too much confidence in the Prime Minister and his advisers to doubt, even for a single moment, that this measure was not absolutely necessary to maintain unity' and solidarity in the government ranks and preserve the peace of the country, threatened by the unavowed ambitions of the group of agitators whom we all know. A plebiscite will thus be held in a few months. I am convinced that the people will welcome it as a truly democratic measure and answer it conscientiously and in the best interest of the nation.
For my part, I approve the principle of this appeal to the people because of the special circumstances which necessitate it, and I understand that the government will submit, after the conclusion of the present debate, a bill which will permit us to examine and determine the details of this plebiscite.
The main motion before the house asks the members for a vote of confidence in this government.
An adverse vote, on whatever ground, would be a condemnation of the policy generally followed by our leaders and an indication of want of confidence in the authority of the Prime Minister.
I congratulate the government on having maintained as the first principle of their war policy that the might of our country and the efficiency of its cooperation with the allied powers must be based on the unity and common action of all sections of her population, for the one purpose dear to all Canadians, namely, the ultimate victory of o-ur forces.
I note with pleasure the wonderful balance given to our war effort, which has been kept free from passions and injustices which were rampant during the last conflict and which it is sought in certain quarters to revive.
I say to the Prime Minister without hesitation that we admire the mastery with which he is guiding the ship of state through the difficulties of all kinds constantly being raised. I wish to assure him of our unswerving confidence and to say that as representative of the *constituency of Verdun, I will vote against both amendments and in favour of the main motion.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will take just a few minutes of the time of the house to state the reasons why I shall vote for the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
The Address-Mr. Denis

Why should I betray the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), when I am convinced that he is the only man who is able, for the present, to administer the country according to the wishes, not only of the electors of the constituency of St. Denis, but of the whole population of Canada? Why should I lack confidence in him when he has protected us since the beginning of the war against disunion, against those who were thirsting for profit and power, against the financiers and the ultra-imperialists? Why should I deny him my support when he thinks the same as we do as regards conscription for overseas service? It would be silly and inconsistent to say: I have so much confidence in King that I am going to vote against him; he has administered the country so well since 1940 that I am going to vote to put somebody else in his place.
Mr. Speaker, it may be interesting to set oneself as the saviour of one's race, as the protector of one's province and constituency, and at the same time to have one's colleagues considered as "followers." But one must beware not to cut off one's nose to spite one's face.
If I vote against the address in reply to the speech from the throne, I will be voting with and for the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson), and if a sufficient number of members from the province of Quebec do the same thing, the government may be defeated, and in all probability the leader of the opposition would be called upon to form a government. With the combined help of the Conservatives, the C.C.F., the Social Crediters, and the few Liberal members who do not see eye to eye with us on the subject of conscription for overseas service, that might well happen and immediately afterwards the house would pass a conscription bill with "blitzkrieg" speed. What a nice gift it would be for my electors of St. Denis and for the country were I to vote along with certain people I know.
Mr. Speaker, it is always wise to ponder the consequences of an act before making the decisive move. It is also advisable not to hurt ourselves when we want to help ourselves.
For the present we must show our confidence in the government by approving in bulk the measures announced in the speech from the throne. Then each one will be examined separately by the house, including the plebiscite. That will be the proper occasion to discuss them.

Therefore I will consider it a pleasure and a duty to support the government by voting for the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I shall vote against all the amendments moved to date, which if adopted would undoubtedly and unfortunately result in a Conservative government, or a national government, or a government directed by the 200 of Toronto, plus a conscription act for service overseas. If I am wrong, I pray God to enlighten me.
Before closing, Mr. Speaker, may I be allowed to read one of de la Fontaine's fables which is chock-full of good sense and seems to befit the occasion.
THE BEAR AND THE GARDEN-LOVER A certain Bear, whose dam had licked him ill,
Dwelt in a lonely forest on a hill.
A new Bellerphon, he shunned his kind,
Till the seclusion, telling on his mind,
Went near to drive him melancholy-mad. Though speech be good, and silence better still,	,	,
And sense consorts not long with solitude. The other animals tabooed;
His unattractive domicile;
And he, for all his bearishness,
Relished isolation less and less.
Meanwhile, in the same neighborhood, There lived a Greybeard, who was likewise bored.
He had a taste for gardening, and adored Both Flora and Pomona, whose employ, Though always pleasant, yields a fuller joy If shared with some congenial friend;
For gardens rarely talk-(except in Fable).
At length, dissatisfied to spend His life in circles purely vegetable.
On day he gave his silent loves the slip In search of livelier companionship.
The Bear, impelled by a like yearning,
Had left his cheerless eminence,
And by an odd coincidence They met each other at a turning.
Tlie Man took fright, but what was to be done?
Twas not the feaintest use to run;
And feeling that on such a case 'Twas 'well to put one's boldest face,
He managed to dissemble his alarm.
The Bear, whose manner failed in courtly charm,	t
Muttered a grumpy invitation.
'Nay,' said the other, won't Your Lordship grace
My humble cot, which you can see from here, And condescend to cheer Of milk and fruit? no doubt a strange collation
For one of your distinguished race,
But 'tis the best I have.' the Bear agreed. They were good friends before they reached the door;	_
And though 'tis better, by the wise man's creed,
To live alone with a bore,
Once there, they got on very well indeed. The Man could garden undisturbed all day, For Bruin had barely two words to say.
He went a-hunting to supply their need; But his great line was shooing flies away

The Address-Mr. Farquhar
From his friend's forehead as a-drowse he lay.	, .	,
Once while the Oldster snored in deep repose,
A bluebottle assailed his nose With such persistence that the Bear At last was driven to despair.
'I'll swat you, ma'am, for this,' he growled- 'here goes!'
Therewith he hurled a brickbat through the air,
Which squashed the fly-but broke the sleep- head.	_	,
His aim was better than his reasoning,
And the result of all his pains Was that his chum lay doornail dead.

An idiot's friend's a dangerous thing:
I'd sooner have a foe with brains.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I had not intended to take part in this debate, but after listening to some statements made by some hon. members and reading certain articles in the press which to my mind are misleading and far from the facts, I feel I should say a few words to present the situation as I see it.
It is true, as some hon. members have said, that we are indeed passing through a most serious time. There never was a time in the history of the world when we had so much at stake as we have to-day; never a time when it was more important that Canada should be united, never a time when it was so necessary that all democratic countries should be united in order that we may put forward our maximum war effort. I am sure that the people will never forget the dark days of Dunkirk, the fall of France, the narrow escape we had from losing our Canadian army. As Lord Halifax said, what a blessing it was that if France was going to fall, she fell as soon as she did! Had she held out a little longer, our Canadian army would have been so far inland that they would have had no possible chance of escape. What a disaster that would have been!
Then came the long year when Britain had to stand alone; not a country in Europe to look to for help, her own manufacturing industry in danger of being destroyed. Therefore she had to look to Canada, Australia, New Zealand and the United States, none of which were in a position to give her very much help. At the beginning of 1941, Britain had not an army worth calling an army, her air force wras no match for the German air force; she was losing the battle of the Atlantic; the enemy were sinking her ships much faster than they could be built. Notwithstanding all this, notwithstanding the tremendous setback we had in the far east and the great sacrifices we shall yet have to make before we get control of the far eastern situation-notwithstanding all this the past year has been a very successful year for Britain and her allies.
Britain won the battle of the air over Britain in the fall of 1940, and this gave her an opportunity to prepare for the expected invasion in the spring of 1941. Britain was all set for the attack, which would have meant tremendous sacrifices of life and property, but she was not called upon to go through that ordeal. Hitler went east to attack Russia, thinking, of course, it would be a short job and then, when he had nothing to fear from Russia, he would return and destroy Britain. But in doing so, as Mr. Churchill said, he made the greatest blunder of his life. The resistance of Greece, Yugoslavia, with the help of Britain, delayed Hitler's plans for six weeks, just long enough to bring winter upon the German armies before they could knock out the Russian army and get possession of the great Russian oilfields last autumn. Russia is putting up a great fight, winning a great victory. She has destroyed much of the German manpower and equipment. She has more trained reserves than Germany, and if she can get the tanks, heavy guns and aeroplanes, she will drive every German out of Russia and defeat Germany on her own soil. The great question is how soon and in what quantities can we get the tanks, heavy guns and aeroplanes across to her. This is the important question to-day.
To hear some hon. members speaking in this house, and to read some of the articles appearing in the press, one would think that there was only one really loyal class in Canada, only one class really interested in the winning of the war, and that this class consisted of the Conservative members of this house and their friends. I should like to tell hon. gentlemen to my left that many Liberals have boys in this war, too. I believe we think just as much of our boys as they do of theirs. I think we are just as much interested in our neighbours' boys as they are. I think we are just as loyal to the principles for which we are fighting as they are, and certainly we have just as much at stake. I like to feel that all men are sincere. I should like to feel that all members of this house are sincere. I should like to feel that the entire press of Canada is sincere. I should like to feel that the Premier of Ontario is sincere; for when we feel that men are sincere we can respect them for their sincerity even though we may disagree with them. But when men have the facts and withhold those facts; when they make statements which they know are not according to the facts, then I must question their sincerity.
The Address-Mr. Farquhar

What are the facts? First, let me say that as far as the Premier of Ontario is concerned, we all know his problem. It is a long-drawn out desire for revenge, without just cause, upon the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mackenzie King), a man who is big enough just to ignore him. By his continued insults, the Premier of Ontario has so belittled himself that he has lost the confidence not only of many of his close friends but of the Liberals of the province of Ontario, and he has lost the respect and confidence of all good thinking men and women throughout the Dominion of Canadd. I am sure that all members of this house, I care not to what party they belong, if they are sincere, fair and reasonable will agree that the all important question to-day is not more men for overseas, however important that may be. The important question to-day is more equipment for the men whom we have overseas at the present time. So far in this war there has not been a battle lost because of shortage of men. Every battle that has been lost so far in this war has been lost because of a shortage of equipment, a shortage of heavy guns, heavy tanks and aeroplanes. Every member of this house knows this statement to be true.
Russia said recently that she had an unlimited number of men, but that her great problem was to equip them with heavy tanks, heavy guns and aeroplanes. China has made the statement that she, too, has an unlimited number of men whom she cannot equip, and that her army in the field is not even yet equipped. Her cry is for more tanks, more heavy guns and more aeroplanes. India now has a million men in her army. She recently stated that she could put eight million men into the fight if only she could get equipment for them. The United States has 130,000,000 people and could put millions of men into her army, but she cannot get equipment for them quickly enough. Canada has over a hundred thousand men in her air force. Our great problem is to get bombing and fighting planes fast enough for them to fight with. Britain's army is not yet fully equipped, because Britain has been doing what Canada has been doing, sending all the equipment she could to Russia, China, Libya and every battle front *where it could be used. I have here a clipping from a Port Arthur newspaper, written by Judge McKay under date of February 2, 1942, right along the line of what I have been saying. It reads:
Japan has a large navy and merchant marine and a very large number of aircraft carriers, bombers and aircraft and will probably attack

British Columbia instead of Australia rvith a view of destroying industries and plants on the Pacific coast both in the United States and Canada.
During 1942, and until the United States can get into maximum production, practically every man should be retained in Canada to defend the Pacific coast and produce as many ships, aircraft, tanks and other mechanized war equipment as possible.
There are apparently over 1,500,000 Polish officers and trained soldiers who were prisoners of war in Russia who are now free and desperately anxious to carry the war into the very heart of Germany as soon as Canada and the United States can furnish them with the necessary clothing, bombers, tanks and necessary equipment. These officers and soldiers have already had experience in this war.
There are millions of men in China and India and elsewhere who are crying out for more mechanized military equipment.
For the sake of all that is precious and priceless the agitation for conscription should be dropped, and as far as possible the capacity to produce agricultural products and mechanized war equipment should be doubled.
In the face of these facts will any reasonable man tell me that the all-important question is the conscription of men, to send all we can overseas, when we cannot equip the men whom we already have over there? Our Canadian soldiers are brave, but is that a reason for sending them to the battle front to face the enemy without the proper equipment? Is it fair to ask the Russians, the Chinese or those brave soldiers from India to go into battle without all the necessary war equipment? These countries are calling to Canada, not for men but for tanks, heavy guns, aeroplanes, ships and all kinds of war equipment. We have the manufacturing industry; we have the raw materials; we have the farm lands to grow the foodstuffs. Before this war is ended, there is a distinct possibility that the industries of Britain may be destroyed.	Britain may have to look to
Canada even more than she looks to-day to supply her with war equipment. There is no question but that there will be a greatly increased demand for foodstuffs, and we shall make a serious mistake if we rob our farmers of experienced farm help. Too many men have been taken from some sections already, and production cannot be kept up if this continues. Our big job, then, at the present time is to equip and feed the millions of trained men who are ready and willing to fight, if they can get the equipment to fight with.
Do not misunderstand me; I am not opposed to conscription if it is necessary. When the time comes when we can equip the men we now have at the battle front, and the voluntary recruiting system to supply a sufficient number of men for reinforcements has

The Address-Mr. Farquhar
failed, I shall be in favour of conscription. And when that day does come, I trust that the conscription of wealth will come also. But I do not think anyone can say that voluntary recruiting has failed, when there are over
400,000	men enlisted for overseas service, and when during the last seven months there was an average of 20,000 a month, including enlistments in all branches of the army. So far as conscription is concerned, the government could do no more than they are now doing, because every training camp in Canada is filled to capacity, and will be for months to come.
So much has been said in the house with regard to the plebiscite that I wish to add only a word. Every hon. member knows both parties gave, their promise that conscription would not be brought in for overseas service during this war. That promise was made not before, but some time after war was declared. Whether or not we individually made the promise, the fact that we supported our leaders who did make the promise commits us just as much as though we made the promise ourselves. Had the government gone ahead and brought in conscription for overseas service, without asking to be released from their promise, there would have been nothing left for me to do but to resign my seat. To my mind that is the only course any hon. member could take. How an hon. member could take any other view, I cannot understand.
Some men who know better are trying to make us believe that the government is attempting to evade responsibility by the taking of the plebiscite. That, of course, is not true. The government is asking to be released from the promise made, in order that it may be able to take on the additional responsibility of bringing in conscription, should it become necessary to do so.
There is one thing more I wish to say before resuming my seat. When this war is W'on, as it will be, and when great sacrifices have been made, do not let us forget what we are fighting for. During the last war some of us who could not go over encouraged the boys by telling them that they were fighting a war to end war; that they would return to a better world, a world in which there would be more equalities of opportunity, a world where men would not have to spend their days living in fear of unemployment; that men with families would not have to live in fear of losing their jobs; that they would not have to live in fear of sickness, or of impoverished old age. Such worry and fear have brought many men and women to early graves.
Yes, during the last war we saw the vision of a better world, and we held that vision up before the boys as they left Canada, and left behind them all they held dear in life. We won the war, but we lost the vision. We settled back in our old ways of living. We passed through a depression, the like of which I trust the people of Canada will never be called upon again to experience.
Of late I have been reading a good deal about Russia; and while I am not a communist and believe in the democratic form of government, still I am convinced we could learn many lessons from the Russian people. I believe the inequality of our system is wrong, and must be changed. The day of special privileges for certain classes in Canada must come to an end. Again we see many of our leaders holding up before us a vision of a better world to live in after this war is over. May we this time make the vision a reality; for land and possessions won, enemies subdued, will count for nothing to the rising generation unless there is a more lasting effect upon the lives and characters of the nation's individuals.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Since the opening of the present session, Mr. Speaker, we have heard, in this house, hon. members from all parties, representing the various parts of Canada, express their views on the momentous problems which we have to solve at the present time. I would like now to give you a sincere statement of my opinion on the matter. I will endeavour to do it in a frank and honest manner without stirring up sentiment or prejudice.
For my part, Mr. Speaker, I must admit that I had a disagreeable surprise on reading in the speech from the throne that the government intended to ask our population, by means of a plebiscite, to be released from any obligation arising out of any past commitments restricting the methods of raising men for military service. I sincerely thought that this question asked of our population during the electoral campaign of 1940, had been answered for the duration of the present parliament and that, consequently, there was no earthly use in putting it again. It is hard to believe that the government will disregard the mandate entrusted to them and that a great majority of the hon. members have already forgotten their solemn pledge to the electors. I cannot believe it, for the answer was too clear-cut, too unanimous, too eloquent. I must say, Mr. Speaker, that I have not forgotten those pledges and that I feel just as honestly bound by them as I did on the evening of March 26, 1940.
The Address-Mr. Bourget

I feel that, in a democracy, where the electors of each constituency give to a person the right to represent them and speak on their behalf, they are entitled at least to the sincerity of their representative as their sole guarantee against deception. For anyone to entertain the contrary opinion would be to deny the elementary principles of democracy. Mr. Speaker, I have faith in democracy and its principles and because of this faith, I would be the last to attempt to destroy it.
I wonder whether the members of the official opposition in this house asking with such eagerness that the government break their pledge are really sincere when they parade their readiness to every sacrifice in order to safeguard democracy. One is entitled to doubt their statement when recalling the actions of their party in past circumstances of a similar nature and when considering the kind of supporters their campaigns draw from outside.
I am not a prophesier of evil, but let me say that they might be the first to lament over the results of their present campaign.
The candidates of their party, following in the footsteps of their leaders, took, before the electors of the whole country, the solemn pledge if they were set in power of never enacting conscription for overseas service. Queer pledge indeed, Mr. Speaker, for during the very first session of this parliament we have witnessed in this house an extremely energetic campaign against the government for the purpose of compelling them to set aside their pledge and enact conscription for overseas service.
They did not ask if our country was well prepared to defend itself; they did not ask how many men were needed for the defence of our coasts and the protection of our civilian population in the hinterland. They did not ask how many men our farmers, our war industries and our shipyards would need for maximum production.
No, for certain people, our first duty was not to defend our own country, but to be at the side of Great Britain.
That is not the way I understand my duty as a Canadian citizen, because I consider that each country's foremost responsibility is, first of all, to assure it own security. Unable to persuade the majority in this house, duly elected by the people, to change their views on the subject, our opponents do not accept defeat so easily; they go outside to the press and the high priests of finance for support. A campaign soon follows, in a certain section of the
	.
country particularly; these people try cunningly and dishonestly to impose their views, under the cloak of patriotism. All means are fair for them; racial prejudice, religious differences, they stop at nothing, as long as they reach their goal; they do not even stop to think that they are in great danger of defeating their own purpose.
You will admit that it is not by seeking the destruction of the present national unity that our war effort will be increased. The citizens of all parts of the country are heartily desirous of contributing to the full measure of their capacity towards the victory of our allies. I would deem it a crime to seek to destroy this noble enthusiasm by undermining national unity for petty purposes.
It has been stated repeatedly by many persons in this house and outside, even last year, that the military act of 1917, enacted by the government of the day, had in fact disrupted national unity. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, is it logical to believe that what was true in 1941 is no longer true in 1942?
For my part, I sincerely believe that the adoption of conscription for overseas service would certainly destroy what all true Canadians have striven to build up since confederation. Are those who now strive to disrupt that national unity and use every means to bring about the enactment of conscription so blind as not to see that this government 'has put forth a maximum effort to help our allies? Let us look around us, let us travel in the various provinces, and we will witness with admiration the exuberant activity that prevails in all our industries producing war material to help our allies.
Is not the speech delivered in this house by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), at the beginning of this session, an accurate summary of the wonderful effort we are putting forth?
Early in January I happened to read in one of the great newspapers of the American metropolis about Canada's share in the present war, and, I frankly admit that, as a Canadian, I was not ashamed of the story told to our neighbours.
Why then, Mr. Speaker, should we abandon the policy we have followed up to the present? Is it not the best one? Have the results not clearly shown that it is? The statements made by some people show a total lack of sense of proportion. How can it reasonably be claimed that with a population of eleven million it is possible to: (1) Supply industry with all the labour it actually needs and may need in greater proportion later on. In the province of Quebec alone there is at present

The Address-Mr. Whitman
a shortage of more than 30,000 bushmen; and everybody knows that our boat-building industry is seeking thousands of experienced workers. (2) To leave to agriculture all the hands essential to its survival.
Already complaints are being heard in the rural centres about the shortage of labour, and many agricultural associations and county councils have sent resolutions to their federal members and to the government asking that farmers' sons be exempted from military service. (3) Supply the country with all the soldiers necessary for its own defence and at the same time send hundreds of thousands of men overseas.
I dare hope, Mr. Speaker, that such a thing shall never occur and that most members of this house agree with me on that point. I respect the opinions of other people. In the present circumstances, everyone should assume his own responsibilities. Personally, Mr. Speaker, I do not fear to assume mine, and I sincerely regret that the government does not continue the policy they have followed since the last election.
The campaign conducted by our opponents here and outside matters little. Personally, I am convinced that the majority of right-minded citizens approve our conduct. Everything was not perfect, I admit, but no one, I think, can logically expect a human organization to be perfect.
That is why I cannot support the policy of the government on the plebiscite. I consider moreover that such a policy is fraught with danger, especially under the present circumstances, when it is so easy to appeal to prejudice and revive old political rancour. In some places, attempts will be made to convince the people that they should vote "yes" under the pretext that the sacrifice will not be equal, and elsewhere a similar vote will be given for the sole purpose of embarrassing the government.
Moreover, should the Tories succeed, in bringing the people to accept conscription, will any one believe, Mr. Speaker, that they would not press their campaign for a union government. I find at page 151 of the debates of this session, a statement showing that our opponents are already preparing a campaign along those lines. Let me quote the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Bruce):
If the Prime Minister is committed on conscription he is equally committed against a national government; consequently, if he is
bound to proceed with a plebiscite, he should also ask to be relieved from a commitment against a national government.
May we not believe, under the circumstances, that we are treading on dangerous ground in proposing such a measure? Are we not going to play into the hands of our opponents?
I am inclined to believe it, for if we give way on one point of our programme, we may later have to give way on another.
So far as I am concerned, Mr. Speaker, I have told my electors that I would fulfill the promises I made at the last election and under the circumstances I do not see why I should alter my course.
The very essence of liberalism compels the Liberal party to let its members be free to express their views, even within the party, and notwithstanding my respect and admiration for my leaders, I regret very much to have to disagree with them about the plebiscite. Consequently, I shall vote against both amend1-ments as well as against the address in reply to the speech from the throne.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at this late hour of the debate I should like to express my congratulations to the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I was greatly impressed by both the subject matter and the splendid delivery of both addresses.
This debate has seemed to me to be both interesting and educational. As a new member, and one not yet well educated in political strategy or intrigue, I have been impressed by the arguments advanced by the opposition to the government.
In the general election of 1940 I found myself elected as a supporter of this government. My political opponent, the late Mr. W. Allan Walsh, was one of Montreal's most public-spiritedi men and one of her finest gentlemen. In many ways it was unfortunate that he had to be defeated.
As a follower of this government I expect still to be able to arrive at decisions dictated by my own conscience. Not being a politician or a strong party man, I felt that I could vote conscientiously and honestly. This has been my aim in the past and shall continue to be my aim in the future.
The debate so far has brought out two important points: one, the government is making a real war effort according to plan; two, even greater efforts must be made in the future.
The effort so far made by Canada has been well made. That is nothing to be smugly satisfied with; but, like all sincere efforts, it is gaining in momentum as it goes along. J
The Address-Mr. Whitman

was particularly impressed by the report of the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) when, last November, he delivered his report to this parliament. He described the result then as the result of the planning of the year before, and promised that, as time went on, a further development would take place and industrial evolution would unfold which would astonish us. I remember well when tanks were not even on order by this department, and now we find this complicated piece of war machinery coming along at several per day. The manufacture of guns, aeroplanes, vehicles of war, et cetera, that we have never tried to manufacture before, has astonished the world, and has proved to us that this government has made and is making a very material contribution according to plan and with the cooperation of both labour and capital, towards winning this war.
Agriculture, lumbering, transportation, mining and fishing are other phases of industry which deserve special mention. Our mines are producing minerals and coal which will eventually bring us victoiy. Our agriculture will in the future be taxed to the utmost but will produce whatever is necessary to feed civilization. Transportation in Canada is doing a splendid job; and right here I should like to pay tribute to those shop workers of our railways who are keeping the equipment in shhpe. When new equipment is not available, the old is kept in service, and developments take place of which the public never hears. But the wheels roll, freight and humans are transported, and, except for some faultfinding when trains are late we pay little attention to details and difficulties. We expect efficiency, and I think we are getting it pretty well all along the line. Each department seems a cog in the wheel of a successful war effort. If one of those cogs should break down, we would, in a short time, >be aware of a serious situation in all departments. If our fishermen caught no fish, or if our lumbering industry were stopped, our entire effort would be slowed down or would become out of step. We have confidence in these phases of our national life, and feel certain they will not fail us. Sometimes little irritations arise that cause inconvenience-a strike here, or a lock-out there-but on the whole the wheels roll on without let-up, and will continue to do so until victory is ours. As long as the cogs of Canadian effort fit, we shall have a wheel that turns efficiently. And this whole Canadian effort, Mr. Speaker, is just another cog in a larger wheel-the wheel of the twenty-six nations now signed to a pact to save Christian civilization as we know it.

If we as Canadians fall down in our effort, the whole cause suffers and is slowed up. We must not fail in our duty.
This brings me to the most contentious point yet discussed in this parliament-the plebiscite. I am not going to justify the causes leading to the undertaking of this plebiscite or the promises made that are being discussed. In fact, I will not attempt at this time to discuss the taking of the plebiscite, but I want to make this definite statement. If this plebiscite carries-and I know it will-I shall expect this government this session to adopt whatever powers are necessary so that our war effort will be the most effective possible. Conscription? Yes, if our war effort demands it, then let us pass it. Conscription is not a Liberal or a Conservative issue; it is bigger than any party or any section of our country. I should like to see our man-power and our woman-power detailed to a position of trust for the duration of the war and know they would be compelled to remain there till victory is won. Our farmers should have detailed to them the help needed to farm efficiently. Our industries should also have the man-power or woman-power required. Conscription-or should I call it compulsory national service?-should be a measure to ensure that our war effort is as effective as it can be with due regard to the desires and demands of the other twenty-five signatory nations of the Washington pact.
Is any political party qualified to tell this government when conscription is necessary? Is there a newspaper in this whole country that can intelligently state that to-day is the day to bring in such a measure, or am I, a member of this house, in a position to demand or insist that the government enact such a law to-day? Surely it would be sheer effrontery for any of us, with the limited knowledge we have at our disposal, even to suggest what is the most desirable course at this time. Even our experts, with all the knowledge they have at their disposal, are puzzled as to what might be the correct course. I believe, however, if we trust those experts and have faith in ourselves and our institutions and work to assist to the maximum the effort being made by Canada, that effort will be one which historians will record as worthy of this generation. Never will it be said that we failed in a time of stress to be effective and loyal both to our traditions and to those other twenty-five nations that are now our allies in this fight for survival.
Much is being said to-day about conscription for overseas service. This really is only one phase of our war effort, and it is my considered opinion that when men are required

The Address-Mr. Whitman
for overseas service they will be obtained. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) is not going to take no for an answer when the need is there. Up to the present we have recruited men for our army voluntarily. We have also raised money voluntarily. We have built tanks, guns, aeroplanes voluntarily. We have raised farm products voluntarily. But if any of these or any other phases of our war effort fail, conscription will be enforced so quickly that even the opposition will be surprised; and as Mr. Menzies told us last year when he addressed the Canadian club here, let us at times say to the government, "Well done; we did not know you had it in you."
I have yet to hear one word of praise from the opposition as to any of our accomplishments. This is unfortunate since the people of Canada are aware of some of our successes and are certain to discount largely the statements of those who depreciate or belittle the results so far obtained. If Sir Robert Borden, Sir Sam Hughes, Sir Joseph Flavelle or the other leaders of the last war effort could see what we have done in this war, I think they would be astounded at the expansion of industry and our success in raising an army. And if we could see what the future holds, if we could visualize how many casualties we might have in the next year, how easy it would be to plan our efforts. But this we do not know; therefore our-effort must be elastic. Our leaders and our government must take whatever steps are considered necessaiy as time elapses to coordinate our effort with our twenty-five allies, so that the entire allied effort will be efficient and successful. For this reason no promises should be made as to what will be done in the future, and promises made in the past must not tie the hands of our government to do Canada's share in the future.
When this plebiscite is taken, as my hon. friend the member for Danforth (Mr. Harris) has said, we must all vote "Ja" overwhelmingly; and after the vote is taken, we must not stop there. As the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) told us, in his excellent address, the government will be free to act and will act in the best interests of the country. Our duty will be to see that such statements are carried into effect, not by threats but by cooperation and by just such debates as are taking place here to-day. In the meantime, trust and confidence in our government is the order. Have confidence in our Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), who has been Prime Minister so well and so long. Even my hon. friend the member for Parkdale (Mr. Bruce) went to some length to tell us, on May 28, 1940, what a good peace-time Prime
Minister he was. I should like to quote what the hon. member for Parkdale says, as reported in Hansard at page 305, May 28, 1940:
I have been a friend of the Prime Minister of Canada for many years and have admired his many excellent qualities. He was prepared, as few in this country have ever been, by long years of education and training in statecraft for public life. He is a man of high character, a man of peace.
Let us also have confidence in our Minister of National Defence, who in my estimation is giving all that he has to fill his position. The evolution of our munitions and supply make it easier to have confidence in our minister of that department. The Minister of Finance must also command our confidence and our cooperation. If any one in Canada talks about boycotting the war loan of 1942 because of some fancied wrong or of a political injustice, then I say that person is doing an immoral act and should be punished. 'This loan must be oversubscribed, and the Minister of Finance must use any means he deems necessary to ensure its success.
I should also like to say a word on the conscription of wealth and industry. To a limited extent we are having conscription of our wealth to-day. Wages and salaries are paying a defence tax; small, I admit, but still a tax.
I was impressed by the suggestion put forward by my hon. friend the member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) when he suggested a compulsory saving plan. That is, if this national defence tax is not producing sufficient revenue, then let us take a larger percentage of the wages. But let a portion of this collection be returned within five or seven years after the war is finished. Possibly a graduated scale of such saving could be adopted, and we could see the smaller incomes taxed a little less and the larger ones a little more. As I remember one speech made in this house, our Minister of Finance was told that his first war loan was a flop even though the amount of money required was received by extending the time of contribution. I suggest to the Minister of Finance that if he considers it necessary, he should do whatever his judgment tells him should be done to conscript accumulated capital or bank balances or money not being used. If our war effort demands it, I know he will not hesitate.
Now as to industry. I was in a plant a short time ago and talked with the superintendent. In the course of our conversation he told me he had been called to the main office that day and instructed to prepare for the production of a complicated piece of war machinery. He replied that he could not
The Address-Mr. Whitman

produce it conveniently owing to labour involved, space required, et cetera. His directors told him to overcome all obstacles, for if he did not, the government would take over the plant and operate it themselves. This, I think, is all that is necessary at present. Rather than conscription we have cooperation detailed by the government. If a greater degree of cooperation becomes necessary, then I feel certain we shall have it.
I remember a few years ago about a contract for Bren guns. I remember the unrest, suspicion and lack of trust in our public men than were created by statements of a politician and of certain papers. An investigation was held, and I remember the result. Hitler must have smiled to see the slowing up of the production of Bren guns due to that investigation. I met Major-General Lafleche at the station at Montreal West last year and congratulated him upon the splendid results that this contract had produced. I told him he must feel satisfied and almost exultant at this success. His reply was that he knew what the result must be eventually and that the people of Canada would appreciate the situation. Why should we tolerate such tactics? I do not suggest control of the press, but I do believe control should be exercised if a paper stirs up unrest, suspicion and lack of confidence merely for political gain. I think the government could very well appoint a controller to insist that the freedom of the press is guaranteed to papers which print only facts and not propaganda that undermines our war effort.
I am not one of those who expect a depression after the war. I do not believe Canadians will ever tolerate a depression such as we had from 1929 to 1938. If we had kept our young men gainfully employed during those years, they would not have become demoralized. Imagine men twenty-five to thirty-five years of age being gainfully employed for the first time in their lives!
Our economy has been wrong. Possibly out of these new price controls now in force in Canada we may be able to work out a basic price so that farmers, lumbermen, fishermen and other primary producers will be able to enjoy a standard of living which will make their callings attractive. This must be done if democracy is to survive. Depressions such as we have known must not again be tolerated. We expect and must receive from our elected representatives great solutions to great problems. Our present-day war effort shows that nothing is impossible if the will to accomplish is there. We must have faith and1 confidence in ourselves and produce results in peace time similar to those we are producing now.
[Mr. Whitman.1
One other matter I should like to touch on is that of national government. The term "national" seems to be used incorrectly. All elected governments here in Ottawa are national governments. What I expect my Conservative friends wish to have is a union government. To this I cannot subscribe. The government of Britain since the last war has been mainly a union government, and its accomplishments are well known. Surely no one can point with pride to all the results of the union activities of the British government since 1923. Even the talents of the present Prime Minister of Great Britain were not used, in fact they seemed to be discovered only when an emergency appeared. The government of Britain is still union, but I believe democracy such as we enjoy in Canada can be stronger and more efficient if we have a loyal, intelligent and effective opposition. Because this is my belief, I believe we should not now consider union government. If all parties and representatives who have been elected to this house will cooperate, our system will continue to give satisfaction.
In closing, I wish to state my position clearly. I will vote for and exert my greatest.effort to have this plebiscite give the government the authority it requires. This, however, will be only one step towards the ultimate goal. I want to see action taken this session, or as soon as possible after the authority asked for has been obtained, and if it is necessary to act before the results of the plebiscite are known, then I want this government to act first and obtain permission afterwards.
On motion of Mr. Lapointe (Lotbiniere) the debate was adjourned.
On motion of Mr. Crerar the house adjourned at 10.45 p.m.
